# Python for Data Structures and Algorithms: a complete guide

This lesson explains Python **as you need it for algorithmic problem solving**: what Python is, how it runs your code, how variables and references really work, every built-in type and operator, control flow and functions, and then every data structure available to you (list, tuple, dict, set, deque, heap and more) with the **time and space complexity of every operation**. Each idea comes with a program you can run.

## 1. What Python is, and why it behaves the way it does

**Python** is a high-level, **dynamically typed**, **garbage-collected** language designed for readability. The standard implementation, **CPython**, first compiles your source to **bytecode** and then runs that bytecode in a virtual machine (an interpreter). There is no separate compile step to run: `python3 file.py` is enough. Because the interpreter does extra work for every operation, Python is typically 10 to 100 times slower than C++ for tight loops, which is why built-in functions written in C (`sum`, `sorted`, `max`, `Counter`) are the fastest way to do bulk work.

| Property | What it means | Consequence |
|---|---|---|
| **Dynamic typing** | A variable has no fixed type; the *value* has one | Short code, but type errors appear at run time |
| **Everything is an object** | Numbers, strings, functions and classes are objects with identity, type and value | You can store functions in lists, pass them as arguments, and so on |
| **Reference semantics** | Variables are *names* bound to objects | Assignment never copies an object; aliasing surprises are common |
| **Garbage collected** | Reference counting plus a cycle detector | No manual memory management |
| **Batteries included** | A large standard library | `collections`, `heapq`, `bisect`, `itertools`, `functools` cover most needs |

### Strengths and weaknesses for interviews

| Strengths | Weaknesses |
|---|---|
| Very concise: more time to think, less to type | Slower than compiled languages; large inputs may time out |
| Arbitrary-precision integers: no overflow | No built-in balanced tree or sorted map |
| Powerful built-ins and comprehension syntax | Recursion limit (default about 1000) |
| Great for prototyping and explaining ideas | Mutable default arguments and aliasing bugs |

## 2. Program structure and input

A Python file runs from top to bottom; there is no required `main`. By convention you put logic in functions and guard the entry point with `if __name__ == "__main__":`. **Indentation** (four spaces) defines blocks; mixing tabs and spaces is an error. For input, `input()` reads one line (slow for big inputs); `sys.stdin.read().split()` reads everything at once and is the standard fast approach.

import sys

def main():
    data = sys.stdin.read().split()
    n, k = int(data[0]), int(data[1])
    nums = list(map(int, data[2:2 + n]))
    print(f"n={n} k={k} sum={sum(nums)}")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
Read every token once, then convert

**How it works.** `sys.stdin.read()` returns the whole input as one string; `.split()` with no arguments splits on any whitespace and drops empties; `map(int, ...)` converts lazily and `list(...)` materialises. Splitting the entire input costs O(total length) once, far cheaper than thousands of `input()` calls.

## 3. Data types in depth

### 3.1 Names, objects and mutability
In Python `x = 5` does not put 5 "inside" `x`. It **binds the name `x` to an object** that represents 5. Every object has an **identity** (`id(x)`), a **type** (`type(x)`) and a **value**. `==` compares values; `is` compares identity. The most important property of a type is whether its objects are **mutable** (can change in place) or **immutable**.

| Immutable (cannot change) | Mutable (can change in place) |
|---|---|
| `int`, `float`, `bool`, `complex` | `list` |
| `str`, `bytes` | `dict` |
| `tuple`, `frozenset` | `set`, `bytearray` |
| `None` | instances of your own classes (by default) |

Only **immutable** objects are hashable by default, which is why tuples can be dictionary keys and lists cannot.

### 3.2 Numbers
* **`int`** has **unlimited precision**: `2 ** 1000` is exact. There is no overflow, so the "modulo 1 000 000 007" step is needed only because a problem asks for it. Large ints are slower (cost grows with the number of digits), so multiplying two 10⁵-digit numbers is not O(1).
* **`float`** is an IEEE 754 64-bit double (about 15-16 digits): `0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3` is `False`. Use `math.isclose` for comparisons, and integers where exactness matters. `float("inf")` is a handy "infinity" for minimum searches.
* **`bool`** is a subclass of `int` (`True == 1`, `True + True == 2`).
* Conversions are explicit: `int("42")`, `int(3.9)` is `3` (truncates toward zero), `float("1.5")`, `str(12)`, `int("101", 2)` is `5`.

### 3.3 Truthiness
In conditions Python treats these as **false**: `False`, `None`, `0`, `0.0`, `""`, `[]`, `()`, `{}`, `set()`. Everything else is true. So `if not nums:` is the idiomatic empty check. Careful: `0` is false, so `if x:` is the wrong test when `0` is a legal value.

### 3.4 Operators

| Operator | Meaning | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `/` | true division | always returns a `float` |
| `//` | floor division | rounds toward **minus infinity**: `-7 // 2 == -4` |
| `%` | modulo | result has the sign of the **divisor**: `-7 % 3 == 2` (unlike C, Java, Go) |
| `**` | power | `pow(a, b, m)` is fast modular exponentiation |
| `and`, `or`, `not` | logic | short-circuit and return one of the operands: `x or default` |
| `==`, `!=`, `<`, ... | comparison | **chainable**: `0 <= i < n` |
| `in`, `not in` | membership | cost depends on the container (see below) |
| `&`, `\|`, `^`, `~`, `<<`, `>>` | bitwise | on unlimited integers; `~x == -x - 1` |
| `:=` | assignment expression ("walrus") | `if (n := len(a)) > 10:` |

Useful built-ins: `abs`, `divmod(a, b)` (both quotient and remainder), `min`, `max`, `sum`, `round` (banker's rounding: `round(2.5) == 2`), `sorted`, `reversed`, `enumerate`, `zip`, `any`, `all`, `len`, `range`, `map`, `filter`.

print(7 // 2, -7 // 2)          # 3 -4   (floor division)
print(-7 % 3)                   # 2
print(2 ** 100)                 # exact big integer
print(pow(3, 200, 1_000_000_007))
print(divmod(17, 5))            # (3, 2)
print(float("inf") > 10**18)    # True: a safe 'infinity' for min-searches
a, b = 3, 8
a, b = b, a                     # swap without a temp
print(a, b)

## 4. Control flow

**Conditionals:** `if / elif / else`; a one-line form `a if cond else b`. Since Python 3.10 there is `match` for pattern matching.

**Loops.**

| Loop | Use it when |
|---|---|
| `for x in iterable:` | iterate values of any iterable (list, string, dict keys, range, generator) |
| `for i in range(n):` | repeat n times (`range(a, b, step)`; `range` does not build a list, O(1) space) |
| `for i, x in enumerate(a):` | you need index and value |
| `for x, y in zip(a, b):` | walk two sequences together |
| `while cond:` | repeat until something changes (binary search, two pointers) |

`break` and `continue` work as usual, and loops have an `else:` clause that runs **only if the loop finished without `break`** (handy for "no match found"). A **comprehension** builds a collection from a loop in one expression: `[x * x for x in a if x % 2 == 0]`, `{x: i for i, x in enumerate(a)}`, `{x % 3 for x in a}`; a generator expression `(x * x for x in a)` does the same lazily with O(1) memory.

**Counting the cost.** A `for` over n items is O(n). A `for` that contains `x in some_list` is O(n²), because `in` on a list scans; replacing the list by a `set` makes the membership test O(1) and the whole loop O(n). Always check the cost of the operation *inside* your loop.

## 5. Functions in depth

A function is defined with `def name(params): ...` and returns a value with `return` (or `None` if it falls off the end). Parameters can have **defaults** (`def f(x, k=3)`), be **keyword-only**, or collect extras with `*args` (tuple) and `**kwargs` (dict). Functions are objects: pass them, store them, return them. A **lambda** is a small anonymous function (`lambda p: p[1]`), common as a `key=` argument. **Closures** capture variables from the enclosing scope (use `nonlocal` to rebind them).

### 5.1 "Pass by object reference"
When you call `f(x)`, the parameter name is bound to **the same object** the caller's name refers to. If the object is **mutable** and the function changes it in place, the caller sees the change. If the function **rebinds** the parameter (`n += 1` on an int, or `n = something_else`), only the local name changes. This is exactly Java's rule, expressed in Python's vocabulary of names and objects. The program below shows it, together with `is` versus `==`, the infamous mutable default argument and shallow versus deep copies. Predict each output first.

import copy

def mutate(nums, n, s, t):
    nums.append(99)        # mutates the caller's list (same object)
    n += 1                 # rebinds a local name; the caller's int is untouched
    s += "!"               # strings are immutable: creates a new local string
    t = t + (4,)           # tuples too

a = [1, 2, 3]; n = 5; s = "hi"; t = (1, 2, 3)
mutate(a, n, s, t)
print(a, n, s, t)                         # [1, 2, 3, 99] 5 hi (1, 2, 3)

x = [1, 2]; y = x                         # two names, ONE list
y.append(3)
print(x, x is y, x == [1, 2, 3])          # [1, 2, 3] True True

p = [1, 2]; q = [1, 2]
print(p == q, p is q)                     # True False  (equal value, different objects)

a1, a2 = 256, 256
b1, b2 = 10**6, 10**6
print(a1 is a2, b1 == b2)                 # True True (small ints are cached; never rely on `is` for numbers)

def bad_default(x, bucket=[]):            # the default list is created ONCE
    bucket.append(x); return bucket
print(bad_default(1), bad_default(2))     # [1, 2] [1, 2]  (shared!)

def good_default(x, bucket=None):
    if bucket is None: bucket = []
    bucket.append(x); return bucket
print(good_default(1), good_default(2))   # [1] [2]

grid = [[1, 2], [3, 4]]
shallow = grid.copy(); shallow[0][0] = 100
deep = copy.deepcopy(grid); deep[1][1] = -1
print(grid)                               # [[100, 2], [3, 4]]  (rows shared with the shallow copy only)
Names and references, mutability, is versus ==, default-argument trap, shallow vs deep copy

### 5.2 Recursion, the call stack and memoisation
Each call uses a stack frame, and CPython limits depth to about **1000** by default (`RecursionError`). Raise it with `sys.setrecursionlimit(10**6)` for moderately deep recursion, or convert to a loop with an explicit stack. For **dynamic programming**, memoise with `functools.lru_cache(None)` (or `functools.cache`): the first call computes and stores the result, later calls with the same arguments return in O(1); arguments must be hashable.

## 6. Strings in depth

A `str` is an **immutable** sequence of Unicode code points (not bytes). Immutable means every "modification" creates a new string, so building a long string with `+=` in a loop is O(n²) in the worst case; collect pieces in a list and `"".join(parts)` once (O(n)). Indexing `s[i]` returns a one-character string (there is no separate `char` type).

### 6.1 Operations and their costs
Let `n = len(s)`, `m = len(t)`.

| Operation | Code | Time | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Length | `len(s)` | O(1) | stored |
| Index | `s[i]` | O(1) | negative indexes count from the end |
| Slice | `s[a:b]` | O(b - a) | **copies**; avoid slicing in recursion on long strings |
| Concatenate | `s + t` | O(n + m) | new string |
| Join a list | `"".join(parts)` | O(total length) | the right way to build strings |
| Compare / equality | `s == t` | O(min(n, m)) | |
| Membership / find | `t in s`, `s.find(t)` | O(n·m) worst | optimised search; `find` returns -1 if absent, `index` raises |
| Split | `s.split()` | O(n) | |
| Reverse | `s[::-1]` | O(n) | |
| Count | `s.count(t)` | O(n) | |
| Hash | `hash(s)` | O(n) once | cached |
| Case, tests | `lower`, `isdigit`, `isalpha` | O(n) | |

**Space:** a string takes about n bytes for ASCII text (1, 2 or 4 bytes per character depending on the widest character) plus about 50 bytes of overhead.

### 6.2 Characters and numbers
`ord("a")` is 97 and `chr(97)` is `"a"`, so letter frequency tables use `ord(c) - ord("a")` as an index into a list of 26 counters, or simply `collections.Counter`. Strings compare **lexicographically** (dictionary order), and `"B" < "a"` because uppercase letters have smaller code points.

def is_palindrome(s: str) -> bool:
    s = "".join(c.lower() for c in s if c.isalnum())
    return s == s[::-1]

print(is_palindrome("A man, a plan, a canal: Panama"))   # True

parts = []
for c in "abcde":
    parts.append(c.upper())
print("-".join(parts))                                    # A-B-C-D-E

counts = [0] * 26
for c in "banana":
    counts[ord(c) - ord("a")] += 1
print(counts[0], counts[13])                              # 3 2
Strings, join and a letter-count list

## 7. Lists in depth (Python's dynamic array)

A `list` is an array of **references** to objects, stored contiguously. Because it holds references, one list can hold mixed types, and `a[i]` is O(1): pointer arithmetic. When the list is full, CPython allocates a larger array (it **over-allocates by about 12.5%** plus a little) and copies the pointers; growth is geometric, so `append` is **amortised O(1)**.

| Operation | Time | Space | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `a[i]`, `a[i] = x` | O(1) | O(1) | negative index from the end |
| `a.append(x)` | amortised O(1) | O(1) | |
| `a.pop()` | O(1) | O(1) | removes the last item |
| `a.pop(0)`, `a.insert(0, x)` | **O(n)** | O(1) | shifts everything; use `collections.deque` |
| `a.insert(i, x)`, `del a[i]`, `a.pop(i)` | O(n) | O(1) | |
| `x in a`, `a.index(x)`, `a.count(x)`, `a.remove(x)` | O(n) | O(1) | linear scan |
| `len(a)` | O(1) | O(1) | |
| `a[i:j]` (slice) | O(j - i) | O(j - i) | creates a new list |
| `a + b`, `a * k` | O(n + m), O(n·k) | same | new list |
| `a.sort()`, `sorted(a)` | O(n log n) | O(1) in place / O(n) | Timsort, stable |
| `a.reverse()` | O(n) | O(1) | |
| `min(a)`, `max(a)`, `sum(a)` | O(n) | O(1) | |
| `a.copy()`, `list(a)` | O(n) | O(n) | shallow |

**Trap:** `[[0] * c] * r` creates `r` references to the *same* inner list. Use `[[0] * c for _ in range(r)]`.

### 7.1 Tuples
A `tuple` is an **immutable** sequence: fixed length, hashable if its items are, slightly smaller and faster than a list. Use tuples for coordinates `(r, c)`, dictionary keys, and returning several values. Unpacking: `r, c = pos`, `first, *rest = items`, and swaps `a, b = b, a`.

a = [5, 2, 9, 1]
a.sort()                          # in place, stable
print(a, a[-1], a[1:3])           # [1, 2, 5, 9] 9 [2, 5]

grid = [[0] * 4 for _ in range(3)]
grid[1][2] = 7
print(grid)

bad = [[0] * 2] * 2               # the classic mistake: both rows are the same list
bad[0][0] = 1
print(bad)                        # [[1, 0], [1, 0]]

pairs = [(3, "c"), (1, "a"), (2, "b")]
pairs.sort(key=lambda p: p[0])
print(pairs)
print(sorted(["bb", "a", "ccc"], key=len, reverse=True))
Lists, slicing, 2-D grids and sorting with a key

## 8. Dictionaries and sets in depth

### 8.1 How a dict works
A `dict` is a **hash table**. For a key, Python computes `hash(key)`, maps it to a slot in an array, and uses **open addressing** (probing other slots on collision) rather than chaining. Since Python 3.7 a dict also remembers **insertion order** (it stores entries in a compact array and keeps a separate index table). The table **resizes** (roughly doubles) when about two-thirds full, so insertion is amortised O(1). A `set` is a dict without values.

**Keys must be hashable**: immutable types whose `hash` never changes while the object lives. Numbers, strings, tuples of hashables and frozen dataclasses are fine; lists, dicts and sets are not. Equal objects must have equal hashes (`1 == 1.0 == True`, so they are the same key).

| Operation | dict | set | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `d[k]`, `d.get(k)`, `k in d` | O(1) average | O(1) | worst case O(n) with adversarial hashes (rare) |
| `d[k] = v`, `s.add(x)` | O(1) amortised | O(1) | |
| `del d[k]`, `s.remove(x)` | O(1) average | O(1) | `d.pop(k, default)`, `s.discard(x)` do not raise |
| iterate | O(n) | O(n) | in insertion order for dict; arbitrary for set |
| `len` | O(1) | O(1) | |
| `s \| t`, `s & t`, `s - t` | | O(len(s) + len(t)) | union, intersection, difference |
| copy | O(n) | O(n) | |
| Space | O(n), about 50-100 bytes per entry | similar | memory heavier than a list |

Handy patterns: `d[k] = d.get(k, 0) + 1`, `collections.Counter(iterable)` (frequency map with `most_common(k)`), `collections.defaultdict(list)` (auto-creates missing values), `d.setdefault(k, []).append(x)`, `sorted(d.items(), key=lambda kv: -kv[1])`. **Do not modify a dict while iterating it** (`RuntimeError`); iterate over `list(d)` instead.

from collections import Counter, defaultdict

freq = Counter("mississippi")
print(freq.most_common(2))                 # [('i', 4), ('s', 4)]

nums, target = [2, 7, 11, 15], 9
seen = {}                                   # value -> index
for i, x in enumerate(nums):
    if target - x in seen:
        print(seen[target - x], i)          # 0 1
        break
    seen[x] = i

groups = defaultdict(list)
for w in ["to", "be", "or", "not"]:
    groups[len(w)].append(w)
print(dict(groups))                         # {2: ['to', 'be', 'or'], 3: ['not']}

visited = set()
visited.add((0, 1))                         # tuples work as set members
print((0, 1) in visited, len(visited))
Counter, two-sum, defaultdict and a set of tuples
Hashable keys, __eq__/__hash__ via dataclass, and a tiny LRU cache

## 9. Stacks, queues, deques and heaps in depth

### 9.1 Stack
Use a plain `list`: `append` pushes and `pop()` pops, both O(1); the top is `a[-1]`. Memory is O(n).

### 9.2 Queue and deque
**Never use `list.pop(0)` as a queue**: it shifts all remaining items, O(n). Use `collections.deque`, a **doubly linked list of fixed-size blocks**: `append`, `appendleft`, `pop`, `popleft` are all **O(1)**; indexing in the middle is O(n); `deque(maxlen=k)` keeps only the last `k` items (a sliding window of recent values for free).

### 9.3 Heap (priority queue)
`heapq` implements a **binary min-heap on top of a normal list**: index `i` has children `2i + 1`, `2i + 2`. `heappush` sifts up and `heappop` sifts down, each at most log n steps; `heap[0]` is the smallest, O(1). `heapify(list)` turns a list into a heap in **O(n)**. For a **max-heap** push negated values, or use `heapq.nlargest(k, a)` / `nsmallest` (O(n log k)). Items are compared as tuples, so `(priority, counter, payload)` avoids comparing payloads that cannot be ordered.

| Operation | list (stack) | deque | heapq | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| push at end | O(1)* | O(1) | `heappush` O(log n) | |
| pop from end | O(1) | O(1) | `heappop` O(log n) | heap pops the **smallest** |
| push/pop at front | **O(n)** | O(1) | n/a | |
| peek | O(1) | O(1) | `h[0]` O(1) | |
| search | O(n) | O(n) | O(n) | |
| build from n items | | | `heapify` O(n) | |
| space | O(n) | O(n) | O(n) | |

### 9.4 Sorted containers
Python has no built-in balanced tree. The `bisect` module keeps a **sorted list**: `bisect_left(a, x)` / `bisect_right(a, x)` find the insertion point in O(log n), and `insort` inserts in O(log n) search plus **O(n)** shifting. For heavy insert/delete workloads interviewers accept `bisect` on a list, or the third-party `sortedcontainers`.

import heapq
from collections import deque
from bisect import bisect_left, bisect_right, insort

stack = [1, 2]; stack.append(3)
print(stack.pop())                         # 3

q = deque([1, 2]); q.append(3)
print(q.popleft(), list(q))                # 1 [2, 3]

h = []
for x in [5, 1, 4]:
    heapq.heappush(h, x)
print(heapq.heappop(h), h[0])              # 1 4

maxh = []
for x in [3, 9, 4]:
    heapq.heappush(maxh, -x)
print(-maxh[0])                            # 9

print(heapq.nlargest(2, [3, 9, 4, 7]))     # [9, 7]

a = [10, 20, 20, 30]
print(bisect_left(a, 20), bisect_right(a, 20))   # 1 3
insort(a, 25); print(a)

## 10. Sorting and searching in depth

`list.sort()` (in place, returns `None`) and `sorted(iterable)` (returns a new list) use **Timsort**: O(n log n) worst case, **stable**, O(n) extra space, and near O(n) on data that is already partly ordered. Choose what to sort by with `key=`, which is called **once per element** (faster than a comparison function): `sorted(words, key=len)`, `sorted(points, key=lambda p: (-p[1], p[0]))` (second field descending, then first ascending; negate numbers, tuples compare element by element). `reverse=True` reverses while keeping stability. For a rarely needed custom comparison use `functools.cmp_to_key`.

Searching: `x in a` on a list is O(n); on a **sorted** list use `bisect` (O(log n)). Binary search by hand needs a `lo`/`hi` loop (see the Binary Search chapter).

## 11. Classes, objects and memory

A **class** defines attributes and methods; an **instance** is created by calling the class. `__init__` initialises; `self` is the instance. `@dataclass` generates `__init__`, `__repr__` and `__eq__` from annotated fields (use `frozen=True` to make instances hashable). If you define `__eq__` you must also define `__hash__` to use objects as dictionary keys. `__slots__` saves memory for millions of small objects.

CPython frees memory by **reference counting** (an object is freed when no name refers to it) and a **cycle detector** for objects that refer to each other. Because everything is an object with a header, a Python `int` takes about 28 bytes and a one-element list about 64 bytes: a list of a million ints uses roughly 36 MB (8 MB of pointers plus the int objects), far more than a C++ `vector<int>` (4 MB). Use `array.array('i')` or `numpy` when memory matters; in interviews just remember that Python structures are heavier.

### 11.1 Linked structures, trees and graphs
Nodes are small classes (or dataclasses) with references. A binary tree node has `val`, `left`, `right`. A graph is stored as an **adjacency list**: `defaultdict(list)` or a list of lists, O(V + E) space; an adjacency matrix is O(V²). Breadth-first search with a `deque` visits every node and edge once: **O(V + E) time, O(V) space**.
Dataclass nodes, list reversal and tree height
A graph as an adjacency dict and breadth-first search

## 12. Errors and edge cases

Python reports problems with **exceptions**: `IndexError` (bad index), `KeyError` (missing dict key), `ValueError` (bad value, e.g. `int("abc")`), `TypeError`, `ZeroDivisionError`, `RecursionError`. Handle them with `try / except / else / finally`. Python's culture prefers **EAFP** ("easier to ask forgiveness than permission": try it and catch the error) to **LBYL** ("look before you leap": check first), but in algorithm code you mostly **prevent** exceptions by handling edge cases:

| Edge case | Typical bug | Defence |
|---|---|---|
| Empty input | `a[0]`, `max([])` raise | `if not a:` first, or `max(a, default=-1)` |
| One element | neighbour comparisons skip it | test n = 1 |
| Duplicates | a dict overwrites an index | use `setdefault` / decide first-wins |
| Negative numbers | `%` and `//` differ from other languages | check with -1 |
| Huge input | O(n²) timeouts | pick O(n) or O(n log n) ideas |
| No answer | returning garbage | return `-1` or `None` consistently |
Exceptions, EAFP versus LBYL and defaults for empty input

## 13. The master complexity cheat sheet

`n` is the number of elements. "Space" is what the structure itself uses.

| Operation | `list` | `tuple` | `dict` | `set` | `deque` | `heapq` list | `str` |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Index `x[i]` | O(1) | O(1) | n/a | n/a | O(n) middle | O(1) | O(1) |
| Append / add at end | O(1)* | n/a | O(1)* | O(1)* | O(1) | `heappush` O(log n) | n/a |
| Insert / pop at front | O(n) | n/a | n/a | n/a | O(1) | n/a | n/a |
| Insert / delete in the middle | O(n) | n/a | O(1)* by key | O(1)* | O(n) | n/a | n/a |
| Pop from end | O(1) | n/a | n/a | n/a | O(1) | `heappop` O(log n) | n/a |
| Search by value (`in`) | O(n) | O(n) | O(1)* by key | O(1)* | O(n) | O(n) | O(n·m) |
| Min / max | O(n) | O(n) | O(n) | O(n) | O(n) | O(1) smallest | O(n) |
| Sort | O(n log n) | n/a | n/a | n/a | n/a | n/a | O(n log n) |
| Iterate | O(n) | O(n) | O(n) | O(n) | O(n) | O(n) | O(n) |
| Space | O(n) | O(n) | O(n), heavier | O(n), heavier | O(n) | O(n) | O(n) |

\* amortised or average.

**What to say in an interview:** "I'll keep a `dict` from value to index. Each lookup and insert is O(1) on average, so one pass is O(n) time and O(n) extra space. The brute force is O(n²) time and O(1) space; I am trading memory for time."

## 14. Pitfalls and idioms checklist

1. `[[0] * c] * r` shares rows: use a comprehension.
2. Never use a mutable default argument; use `None`.
3. `list.pop(0)`, `insert(0, x)` and `x in list` are O(n): use `deque` and `set`.
4. Use `==` for values and `is` only for `None`.
5. `-7 // 2 == -4` and `-7 % 3 == 2`: floor semantics differ from C, Java and Go.
6. Slicing copies; do not slice repeatedly inside recursion.
7. Do not modify a list or dict while iterating it.
8. `sort()` returns `None`: `a = a.sort()` loses the list.
9. Float comparison: `math.isclose`; avoid floats for exact counting.
10. Use `enumerate` and `zip` instead of index arithmetic.
11. Raise the recursion limit or convert to iteration for deep recursion.
12. A `dict` iterates in insertion order; a `set` does not.
13. Keys must be hashable: convert lists to tuples.
14. Use `Counter`, `defaultdict`, `heapq`, `bisect` and `itertools` instead of writing them by hand.

## 15. A reusable solution template
Template: parse, call a pure function, print

## 16. How Python compares with the other languages in this chapter

| Topic | Python | Java | C++ | Go |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Integer overflow | never | wraps | undefined (signed) | wraps |
| Dynamic array | `list` | `ArrayList` | `vector` | slice |
| Hash map | `dict` | `HashMap` | `unordered_map` | `map` |
| Heap | `heapq` (min) | `PriorityQueue` (min) | `priority_queue` (max) | `container/heap` |
| Sorted map | none | `TreeMap` | `map` | none |
| Speed (loops) | slowest | fast | fastest | fast |

## 17. Practice plan

1. Re-type every program from memory, then change the input so it breaks, and explain why.
2. Solve [Pair With Target Sum](/problems/pair-with-target-sum), [Anagram Groups](/problems/anagram-groups), [Merge Meeting Slots](/problems/merge-meeting-slots) and [Island Counter](/problems/island-counter) in Python.
3. For each structure you use, say its insert, delete, search and iterate cost aloud, and say why.

# C++ for Data Structures and Algorithms: a complete guide

This lesson explains C++ **as you need it for algorithmic problem solving**: how a C++ program is built and runs, every common data type and its limits, the operators and control flow, functions and the three ways to pass arguments, pointers and references, and then every container of the **Standard Template Library (STL)** with its **time and space complexity for every operation**. Every program was compiled and run.

## 1. What C++ is, and why it behaves the way it does

**C++** is a **compiled, statically typed, multi-paradigm** language that gives you control close to the hardware while offering high-level abstractions. Building a program has three steps: the **preprocessor** expands `#include` and macros; the **compiler** translates each source file into machine code (object files); the **linker** joins them into an executable. There is no virtual machine and no garbage collector, so a well-written C++ program is among the fastest you can write, and memory use is predictable.

| Property | What it means | Consequence |
|---|---|---|
| **Compiled to native code** | Runs directly on the CPU | Fastest runtime; a compile step before running |
| **Statically typed** | Types are fixed at compile time | Type errors are compile errors; use `auto` to let the compiler deduce |
| **Value semantics** | Assigning or passing a variable **copies** it by default | Big containers are copied unless you pass by reference |
| **Manual / RAII memory** | You decide object lifetime; destructors run when scope ends | No GC pauses; but dangling pointers and leaks are possible |
| **Undefined behaviour (UB)** | Some mistakes have no defined result | Out-of-range indexing, signed overflow and uninitialised reads can "work" in tests and fail later |
| **Templates** | Code generic over types, resolved at compile time | The STL containers and algorithms are templates |

### Strengths and weaknesses for interviews

| Strengths | Weaknesses |
|---|---|
| Fastest of the common interview languages | Easy to cause undefined behaviour |
| A powerful STL: containers, `sort`, `lower_bound`, `accumulate` | Error messages are long and cryptic |
| Value semantics: no hidden boxing | You must think about copies, references and lifetimes |
| Standard in competitive programming and systems roles | More syntax to remember than Python or Go |

## 2. Program structure and input

A C++ program has a `main` function returning `int` (0 means success). `#include <vector>` brings in a header; `using namespace std;` lets you write `vector` instead of `std::vector` (fine in interviews). Compile with `g++ -std=c++17 -O2 main.cpp -o main` or `clang++`, run `./main`. Input and output use the streams `cin` and `cout`. By default these are synchronised with C's `stdio`, which makes them slow; the two lines `ios::sync_with_stdio(false); cin.tie(nullptr);` remove that cost. Print newlines with `'\n'`, not `endl` (`endl` also flushes, which is slow).

> **Portability note.** You will see `#include <bits/stdc++.h>` in competitive code: a GCC-only header that includes everything. It does not exist on macOS/Clang, so this lesson includes the specific headers; that is also the professional habit.
Fast input with cin and a vector

**How it works.** `cin >> n` skips whitespace and parses an integer; a failed parse sets an error state. `vector<long long> a(n)` creates `n` zero-initialised elements; `for (auto &x : a)` iterates by **reference**, so assigning to `x` would change the vector (without `&` you would modify a copy).

## 3. Data types in depth

### 3.1 Fundamental types

| Type | Typical size | Typical range | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `bool` | 1 byte | `true`, `false` | |
| `char` | 1 byte | -128..127 or 0..255 (implementation-defined) | a small integer; also a character |
| `short` | 2 bytes | ±32,767 | |
| `int` | 4 bytes | -2,147,483,648 .. 2,147,483,647 | the default integer; use `INT_MAX` from `<climits>` |
| `long long` | 8 bytes | about ±9.2 × 10¹⁸ | guaranteed at least 64 bits; use `LLONG_MAX` |
| `unsigned int`, `unsigned long long` | 4, 8 bytes | 0 .. 4.29 × 10⁹, 0 .. 1.8 × 10¹⁹ | wraps around modulo 2ⁿ |
| `float`, `double` | 4, 8 bytes | ~7 and ~15-16 significant digits | IEEE 754 |
| `size_t` | 8 bytes on 64-bit | unsigned | the type of `.size()` and `sizeof` |

The standard fixes only *minimum* sizes; the numbers above hold on mainstream 64-bit compilers. `<cstdint>` gives exact-width types (`int32_t`, `int64_t`, `uint8_t`).

### 3.2 Initialisation and `auto`
**Uninitialised local variables contain garbage**; always initialise: `int x = 0;` or `int x{};`. Global and static variables are zero-initialised. `auto x = 5;` deduces `int`; `auto& r = v[0];` a reference; `for (const auto& s : strings)` avoids copying each string.

### 3.3 Conversions
* **Implicit** conversions can silently lose information: `int x = 3.9;` gives 3 (truncation).
* **Integer promotion:** `char` and `short` become `int` in arithmetic.
* Mixing signed and unsigned is dangerous: in `int a = -1; unsigned b = 1; a < b` the `-1` is converted to a huge unsigned number, so the comparison is **false**.
* Use explicit casts, preferably `static_cast<long long>(x)`, or the C-style `(long long)x`.

### 3.4 Overflow (very important)
* **Signed integer overflow is undefined behaviour.** `INT_MAX + 1` is not guaranteed to wrap; the optimiser may assume it never happens and silently produce wrong code.
* **Unsigned overflow wraps** modulo 2ⁿ (well-defined).
* Therefore: use `long long` whenever a value might exceed about two billion, and **widen before multiplying**: `1LL * a * b`.
* `v.size()` is **unsigned**: `v.size() - 1` on an empty vector is a huge number, and `for (int i = 0; i < v.size(); i++)` mixes signed/unsigned. Cast: `(int)v.size() - 1`.

Floating point behaves as in every language: `0.1 + 0.2 != 0.3`; compare with a tolerance; `1.0 / 0` is infinity, but **integer division by zero is undefined behaviour**. Integer division truncates toward zero and `%` has the sign of the left operand (`-7 / 2 == -3`, `-7 % 3 == -1`); a non-negative modulo is `((a % m) + m) % m`.

## 4. Operators and control flow

| Group | Operators | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Arithmetic | `+ - * / %` | `/` on ints truncates toward zero |
| Comparison | `== != < <= > >=` | `<=>` (C++20) returns the ordering |
| Logical | `&& \|\| !` | short-circuit |
| Bitwise | `& \| ^ ~ << >>` | `x & (x - 1)` clears the lowest set bit; `1 << k` is 2ᵏ (use `1LL << k` for k ≥ 31) |
| Assignment | `= += -= ...` | |
| Increment | `++ --` | prefix returns the new value, postfix the old |
| Conditional | `c ? a : b` | |

**Conditionals:** `if / else if / else`, `switch` (needs `break`, otherwise execution *falls through*). **Loops:** `for (int i = 0; i < n; i++)`, range-based `for (auto x : container)`, `while`, `do { } while`. `break`, `continue`, and `goto` exist. Ranges can be iterated by index, by iterator, or with a range-based `for`.

**Counting the cost.** A loop over n elements is O(n); nested loops over the same data O(n²); a loop that halves the range O(log n). Two pointers moving forward at most n times each is O(n) in total.

## 5. Functions, references and pointers

### 5.1 Three ways to pass an argument
| Style | Syntax | Meaning | Cost |
|---|---|---|---|
| **By value** | `void f(vector<int> v)` | the function gets a **copy** | O(size of the object) |
| **By reference** | `void f(vector<int>& v)` | the function works on the caller's object | O(1) |
| **By const reference** | `void f(const vector<int>& v)` | by reference, but read-only | O(1) |
| **By pointer** | `void f(int* p)` | an address; may be `nullptr` | O(1) |

**Rule of thumb:** pass small types (`int`, `double`, `char`) by value and everything bigger by `const&`. Passing a big `vector` or `string` by value inside a recursive function is the classic accidental O(n) per call.

### 5.2 References and pointers
A **reference** (`int& r = x;`) is another name for an existing variable; it cannot be reseated or null. A **pointer** (`int* p = &x;`) stores an address; `*p` reads or writes the target, `p->field` accesses a member, `nullptr` means "points to nothing" (dereferencing it is UB). An array name **decays** to a pointer to its first element, and `p[i]` equals `*(p + i)`. Memory from `new` must be released with `delete` (`new[]` with `delete[]`); modern code uses **RAII** (a vector, a string, or `std::unique_ptr`/`make_unique`, which free memory automatically when they go out of scope).

Run this program and predict every line first:
Pass by value, reference, const reference and pointer; copies; arrays and pointers

### 5.3 Recursion and the call stack
Each call needs a stack frame; the default stack (about 1 to 8 MB) supports roughly 10⁴ to 10⁵ frames depending on frame size, after which the program crashes with a segmentation fault. Convert very deep recursion to a loop with an explicit `stack`. Lambdas `[&](int x) { ... }` capture variables from the surrounding scope (`&` by reference, `=` by copy); they are the usual way to write comparators and local helper functions.

## 6. Strings in depth

`std::string` is a **mutable** sequence of `char` stored contiguously (plus a terminating `'\0'`). Most implementations use **small-string optimisation**: very short strings live inside the object without heap allocation. Strings have **value semantics**: `string b = a;` copies. `s[i]` is O(1) with no bounds check (`s.at(i)` checks and throws), `+=`/`push_back` is amortised O(1) per character, and you can modify characters in place (`s[0] = 'J'`).

### 6.1 Operations and their costs (`n = s.size()`, `m = t.size()`)

| Operation | Code | Time | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Length | `s.size()` | O(1) | unsigned `size_t` |
| Index | `s[i]` | O(1) | no bounds check |
| Append character | `s.push_back(c)`, `s += c` | amortised O(1) | |
| Append string | `s += t` | O(m) amortised | |
| Concatenate to a new string | `s + t` | O(n + m) | |
| Substring | `s.substr(pos, len)` | O(len) | **copies** |
| Compare | `s == t`, `s < t` | O(min(n, m)) | lexicographic |
| Find | `s.find(t)` | O(n·m) worst | returns `string::npos` if absent |
| Insert / erase in the middle | `s.insert(i, t)`, `s.erase(i, k)` | O(n) | shifts |
| Reverse | `reverse(s.begin(), s.end())` | O(n) | in place |
| Convert | `to_string(x)`, `stoi(s)`, `stoll(s)` | O(length) | `stoi` throws on bad input |
| Space | | O(n) | plus a small header |

`char` arithmetic: `c - 'a'` is 0..25 for lowercase letters; `c - '0'` converts a digit; `isdigit`, `isalpha`, `tolower` live in `<cctype>`. Use a plain array `int cnt[26]` for letter frequencies: O(1) update, 104 bytes.

## 7. Arrays and `vector` in depth

### 7.1 Built-in arrays and `std::array`
A built-in array `int a[100];` has a size fixed at compile time, lives on the stack (large ones, say a million ints, can overflow the stack: make them `static` or global, or use a vector), is **uninitialised** unless you write `= {0}`, and has no bounds checking. `std::array<int, N>` is the same with a nicer interface.

### 7.2 `vector<T>`: the dynamic array
`vector` stores elements **contiguously** on the heap and tracks `size()` (elements) and `capacity()` (room before reallocation). When full, `push_back` allocates a larger block (GCC doubles the capacity, others use 1.5×), **moves or copies every element** (O(n) for that call) and frees the old block. Geometric growth makes the *average* `push_back` **amortised O(1)**. Because storage is contiguous, indexing is O(1) and iteration is cache-friendly. Call `reserve(n)` in advance if you know the final size to avoid regrowth.

| Operation | Time | Space | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `v[i]`, `v.at(i)` | O(1) | O(1) | `at` checks bounds |
| `push_back`, `emplace_back` | amortised O(1), worst O(n) | O(1) amortised | |
| `pop_back` | O(1) | O(1) | |
| `insert(it, x)`, `erase(it)` | O(n) | O(1) | shifts the tail; **invalidates iterators** |
| `front()`, `back()`, `size()`, `empty()` | O(1) | O(1) | |
| `clear()` | O(n) (destroys elements) | capacity kept | |
| `resize(k)` | O(k) | | |
| `find` (`std::find`) | O(n) | O(1) | |
| `sort` | O(n log n) | O(log n) stack | introsort, not stable |
| Copy (`vector b = a;`) | O(n) | O(n) | deep copy |
| Whole structure | | O(n) | capacity may be up to 2× |

**2-D vectors:** `vector<vector<int>> g(r, vector<int>(c, 0));` allocates `r` separate rows (each `O(c)`), total O(r·c) space.

**Iterator invalidation.** After `push_back` (when it reallocates), `insert` or `erase`, previously obtained iterators and references into the vector may be invalid. Do not keep them across such calls; erase while looping by index or by using the iterator returned from `erase`. The erase-remove idiom removes by value: `v.erase(remove(v.begin(), v.end(), x), v.end());` in O(n).

Other sequence containers: `deque<T>` (O(1) at both ends, O(1) random access, stored in blocks), `list<T>` (doubly linked: O(1) insert/erase at a known iterator, but O(n) access and poor cache behaviour), `forward_list<T>` (singly linked).
vector, 2-D vector, erase/insert, pairs and numeric helpers

## 8. Associative containers in depth

### 8.1 Ordered: `map`, `set`, `multimap`, `multiset`
These are **balanced binary search trees** (typically red-black trees). Keys are kept sorted, so iteration yields ascending order, and the cost of every operation is **O(log n)**. They also answer *nearest-key* questions: `lower_bound(x)` is the first key ≥ x, `upper_bound(x)` the first key > x, `begin()` is the minimum and `prev(end())` the maximum. Each node is a separate allocation, so they use roughly 32 to 48 bytes of overhead per element. A key type needs `operator<` (`pair`, `tuple`, `string` already have it).

### 8.2 Hash-based: `unordered_map`, `unordered_set`
These are **hash tables with chaining**: an array of buckets, each a linked list of entries. The hash of a key chooses the bucket; when the **load factor** (entries ÷ buckets) exceeds 1.0 the table **rehashes** (grows and re-inserts). Average cost of insert, find and erase is **O(1)**, but the worst case is O(n) if many keys collide. Iteration order is arbitrary. Only types with a hash and `operator==` can be keys; `int`, `long long`, `string` work out of the box. For `pair<int,int>` or a struct you write a hash functor (see below), use an ordered `set<pair<int,int>>`, or encode `r * cols + c` into one `long long`.

### 8.3 Operations and costs

| Operation | `unordered_map/set` | `map/set` |
|---|---|---|
| insert, `emplace` | O(1) average, O(n) worst | O(log n) |
| `find`, `count`, `contains` (C++20) | O(1) average | O(log n) |
| `erase(key)` | O(1) average | O(log n) |
| `operator[]` | O(1) average (**inserts a default if missing**) | O(log n) (inserts) |
| min / max key | O(n) | O(1) at `begin()` / last |
| `lower_bound`, `upper_bound` | not available | O(log n) |
| iterate | O(n + buckets), arbitrary order | O(n), sorted |
| space | O(n), a node per entry plus the bucket array | O(n), a node per entry |

**Trap:** `m[key]` creates the entry if it does not exist, which is perfect for counting (`cnt[x]++`) but a bug (and slower) when you only want to test existence: use `m.find(key) != m.end()` or `m.count(key)`.
Counting, two-sum, ordered map and set boundaries
Custom keys: operator==, a hash functor, pairs in set, encoded coordinates

## 9. Stacks, queues, deques and heaps in depth

### 9.1 Container adaptors
`stack<T>`, `queue<T>` and `priority_queue<T>` are **adaptors**: thin wrappers around `deque` (the default for stack and queue) or `vector` (for the priority queue) that expose only the operations of the abstract type.

| Structure | LIFO / FIFO / priority | Methods | Underlying |
|---|---|---|---|
| `stack<T>` | LIFO | `push`, `pop`, `top`, `empty`, `size` | `deque` |
| `queue<T>` | FIFO | `push`, `pop`, `front`, `back` | `deque` |
| `deque<T>` | both ends | `push_front/back`, `pop_front/back`, `[]` | blocks |
| `priority_queue<T>` | largest first | `push`, `pop`, `top` | `vector` + heap algorithms |

**`pop()` returns nothing** in C++: read `top()` or `front()` first, then pop. Calling `top`/`pop` on an empty container is undefined behaviour, so check `empty()`.

### 9.2 How the heap works
`priority_queue` keeps a binary heap in a vector using `push_heap`/`pop_heap`: element `i` has children `2i + 1` and `2i + 2`; insertion sifts up (at most log n swaps), removal of the top sifts down (at most log n swaps), `top()` is O(1), and building a heap from n elements (`make_heap`, or the constructor taking a range) takes **O(n)**. The default is a **max**-heap; for a min-heap write `priority_queue<int, vector<int>, greater<int>>`. For pairs, `greater<>` and `pair`'s lexicographic order make `(distance, node)` Dijkstra queues easy. There is no `decrease_key`: push a new entry and skip stale ones when popped.

### 9.3 Operations and costs

| Operation | `stack` / `queue` / `deque` | `priority_queue` | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| push | O(1) amortised | O(log n) | |
| pop | O(1) | O(log n) | |
| top / front | O(1) | O(1) | |
| search | O(n) (not supported by adaptors) | O(n) (not supported) | |
| build from n items | O(n) | O(n) via `make_heap` | |
| space | O(n) | O(n) | |
Stack, queue, heaps, Dijkstra-style pair heap and deque

## 10. Algorithms from `<algorithm>` and `<numeric>`

| Function | Purpose | Time | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `sort(b, e [, cmp])` | sort a range | O(n log n) | introsort: quicksort + heapsort fallback; **not stable** |
| `stable_sort` | stable sort | O(n log n) | uses extra memory |
| `partial_sort`, `nth_element` | k smallest / k-th element | O(n log k), O(n) average | `nth_element` is quickselect |
| `reverse`, `rotate`, `unique`, `remove` | rearrange | O(n) | `unique` needs sorted input |
| `min_element`, `max_element`, `accumulate`, `count`, `find` | scan | O(n) | `accumulate(b, e, 0LL)` sums with a `long long` start |
| `lower_bound`, `upper_bound`, `binary_search`, `equal_range` | search a **sorted** range | O(log n) on random-access iterators | |
| `next_permutation` | next lexicographic permutation | O(n) per call | enumerates all permutations |
| `swap`, `iota`, `fill`, `copy` | utilities | O(n) | `iota` fills 0, 1, 2, ... |

A **comparator** must define a **strict weak ordering**: use `<`, never `<=` (a non-strict comparator can crash `sort`). Write comparators as lambdas. On a sorted range, `lower_bound(v.begin(), v.end(), x) - v.begin()` is the index of the first element ≥ x.

## 11. Structs, classes and the object model

A `struct` is a class whose members are public by default. Constructors initialise; **destructors** run automatically when an object goes out of scope (RAII). A struct of plain data copies member by member. Use `new`/`delete` or smart pointers for linked structures. **Move semantics** (C++11) let containers transfer ownership of heavy objects cheaply instead of copying (`push_back(std::move(x))`); `emplace_back(args...)` constructs in place.

### 11.1 Linked lists and trees
A node holds a value and pointers. Always check for `nullptr` before dereferencing. Insert/delete after a known node is O(1); reaching the i-th node is O(i). Recursion mirrors the tree shape; the height of a tree with n nodes is between log n and n, which is also the recursion depth.
Linked list reversal and tree height with raw pointers

### 11.2 Graphs
Store a graph as an **adjacency list** `vector<vector<int>> adj(n)` (O(V + E) space) or, for weighted edges, `vector<vector<pair<int,int>>>` of `(neighbour, weight)`. An adjacency matrix `vector<vector<int>>` is O(V²). Breadth-first search with a `queue` visits each vertex and edge once: **O(V + E) time, O(V) space**, and gives shortest paths in an unweighted graph.
A graph as vector<vector<int>> and breadth-first search

## 12. Errors and edge cases

C++ has exceptions (`throw`, `try`, `catch`) used by the standard library (`stoi` throws `invalid_argument` or `out_of_range`, `vector::at` throws `out_of_range`), but the core language mostly leaves mistakes **undefined**: indexing outside a vector with `[]`, dereferencing `nullptr`, reading an uninitialised variable and signed overflow compile fine and may appear to work. Tools that help: compile with `-Wall -Wextra`, and test with `-fsanitize=address,undefined`.

| Edge case | Typical bug | Defence |
|---|---|---|
| Empty container | `v[0]`, `*max_element` on empty is UB | check `empty()` first |
| `size() - 1` | unsigned wrap | cast to `int` |
| Overflow | `int` sum/product | `long long`, `1LL * a * b` |
| Negative modulo | `-7 % 3 == -1` | `((a % m) + m) % m` |
| Missing map key | `m[k]` inserts | use `find` / `count` |
| Iterator invalidation | erase/insert while iterating | use returned iterators or indexes |
| Uninitialised variable | garbage values | initialise everything |
Exceptions, checked access with at(), limits and edge cases

## 13. The master complexity cheat sheet

`n` is the number of elements.

| Operation | `vector` | `deque` | `list` | `unordered_map/set` | `map/set` | `priority_queue` | `string` |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Access by index | O(1) | O(1) | O(n) | n/a | n/a | n/a | O(1) |
| Push at back | O(1)* | O(1) | O(1) | O(1)* insert | O(log n) | O(log n) | O(1)* |
| Push / pop at front | O(n) | O(1) | O(1) | n/a | n/a | n/a | O(n) |
| Insert / erase in the middle | O(n) | O(n) | O(1) at iterator | O(1)* by key | O(log n) | n/a | O(n) |
| Pop at back | O(1) | O(1) | O(1) | n/a | n/a | O(log n) | O(1) |
| Search by value | O(n) | O(n) | O(n) | O(1)* | O(log n) | O(n) | O(n·m) |
| Min / max | O(n) | O(n) | O(n) | O(n) | O(1) | O(1) top | O(n) |
| Sort | O(n log n) | O(n log n) | `list::sort` O(n log n) | n/a | already sorted | n/a | O(n log n) |
| Space | O(n) | O(n) | O(n) + pointers | O(n) + nodes | O(n) + nodes | O(n) | O(n) |

\* amortised or average.

**What to say in an interview:** "I'll use an `unordered_map` from value to index: each lookup and insert is O(1) on average, so one pass is O(n) time with O(n) extra space. The brute force is O(n²) time and O(1) space; I'm trading memory for time."

## 14. Pitfalls and idioms checklist

1. `v.size() - 1` on an empty vector wraps; cast to `int`.
2. Signed overflow is undefined: use `long long`, `1LL * a * b`.
3. `m[key]` inserts a default; use `find`/`count` to test.
4. Pass big objects by `const&`; accidental copies hide O(n) costs.
5. `v[i]` is unchecked; debug with `at()` or sanitizers.
6. Initialise variables; locals hold garbage.
7. Comparators use strict `<`.
8. Iterators are invalidated by `insert`, `erase` and reallocation.
9. `-7 / 2 == -3` and `-7 % 3 == -1`; normalise the modulo.
10. `top()`/`front()`/`pop()` on an empty adaptor is undefined.
11. A large local array can overflow the stack: use a vector or a global.
12. Use `'\n'` instead of `endl`; disable `stdio` sync for fast I/O.
13. `1 << 31` overflows an `int`; write `1LL << k`.
14. `unordered_map` can be slow with adversarial keys; `map` is the safe fallback.

## 15. A reusable solution template
Template: parse, call a pure function, print

## 16. How C++ compares with the other languages in this chapter

| Topic | C++ | Java | Python | Go |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Memory | manual / RAII | GC | GC | GC |
| Dynamic array | `vector` | `ArrayList` | `list` | slice |
| Hash map | `unordered_map` | `HashMap` | `dict` | `map` |
| Sorted map | `map` | `TreeMap` | none | none |
| Heap | `priority_queue` (max) | `PriorityQueue` (min) | `heapq` (min) | `container/heap` |
| Integer overflow | UB (signed) | wraps | none | wraps |
| Speed | fastest | fast | slowest | fast |

## 17. Practice plan

1. Re-type each program, then deliberately break it (index out of range, a forgotten `&`) and watch what happens, ideally with `-fsanitize=address,undefined`.
2. Solve [Pair With Target Sum](/problems/pair-with-target-sum), [Kth Largest](/problems/kth-largest), [Cheapest Route](/problems/cheapest-route) and [Course Order](/problems/course-order) in C++; write the time and space complexity of each.
3. Memorise `sort`, `lower_bound`, `priority_queue`, `unordered_map`, `accumulate`, `reverse` and `next_permutation`: they cover most interview needs.

# C# for Data Structures and Algorithms: a complete guide

This lesson explains C# **as you need it for algorithmic problem solving**: what C# and .NET are and how a program runs, every numeric type and the overflow rules, value types versus reference types (the most important idea in C#), control flow, methods and parameter passing, strings, and every collection in `System.Collections.Generic` with the **time and space complexity of every operation**.

> **Verification note.** The Java, Python, C++, JavaScript and TypeScript lessons in this chapter were compiled/type-checked and run before publishing. This machine has no .NET SDK, so every C# program here was written carefully against the documented APIs (.NET 8, C# 12) but **has not been executed**. Create a console project (`dotnet new console`), paste a program, run it, and report anything that does not compile.

## 1. What C# is, and why it behaves the way it does

**C#** is a modern, statically typed, object-oriented and functional-friendly language created by Microsoft for the **.NET** platform. The compiler translates C# into **IL** (intermediate language) stored in assemblies; the **CLR** (Common Language Runtime) **JIT-compiles** IL to machine code as the program runs and manages memory with a **generational garbage collector** (young objects are collected cheaply and often, old ones rarely). C# is used for backend services (ASP.NET), desktop software, games (Unity) and cloud tools.

| Property | What it means | Consequence |
|---|---|---|
| **Statically typed** | Types are checked at compile time | Type mistakes are compile errors; `var` infers the type |
| **Value types vs reference types** | `int`, `struct`, tuples are values (copied); `class`, arrays, strings, collections are references | Assignment semantics differ; this explains most surprises |
| **Garbage collected** | Unreachable objects are freed automatically | No manual freeing |
| **Rich standard library** | Collections, LINQ, async, a built-in `PriorityQueue` | Most structures exist already |
| **Nullable reference types** | The compiler tracks which references may be `null` | Fewer `NullReferenceException`s |

### Strengths and weaknesses for interviews

| Strengths | Weaknesses |
|---|---|
| Consistent, well-named collections and LINQ | More ceremony than Python |
| Built-in `PriorityQueue`, `SortedSet`, `SortedDictionary` | `int` arithmetic **wraps silently** by default |
| Value types and `struct`s avoid allocations | `Dictionary` indexer throws on a missing key |
| Great tooling and type safety | No built-in max-heap flag (use a comparer) |

## 2. Program structure and input

Modern C# (version 9+) allows **top-level statements**: the file's statements form the program, with no `class Program` or `Main`, and you can declare methods ("local functions", marked `static`) and types after them. Run with `dotnet run`. Read input with `Console.ReadLine()` (returns `null` at end of input; the `!` tells the compiler you expect a value). `string.Split(' ', StringSplitOptions.RemoveEmptyEntries)` splits on spaces; `int.Parse` converts (throws `FormatException` on bad text, while `int.TryParse` returns a bool). For large input wrap `Console.In` in a `StreamReader` with a big buffer; `Console.WriteLine` per line is slow, so use a `StringBuilder`.

**How it works.** `Select(int.Parse)` is **LINQ**: it lazily maps each string to an int; `ToArray()` runs the query once and stores the result. LINQ methods are convenient and allocate small objects; in a hot loop a plain `for` is faster.

## 3. Data types in depth

### 3.1 Value types and reference types
This is the central idea in C#.

| | **Value types** | **Reference types** |
|---|---|---|
| Examples | `int`, `long`, `double`, `bool`, `char`, `decimal`, `struct`, `enum`, tuples `(int, int)` | `class`, `string`, arrays, `List<T>`, `Dictionary<K,V>`, delegates |
| A variable holds | the value itself | a reference to an object on the heap (or `null`) |
| Assignment `b = a` | **copies** the value | copies the **reference**: both names point to one object |
| Default value | zero / false | `null` |
| `==` | compares values | identity by default (but `string` and records compare content) |

Locals of value types usually live on the stack (or inside the object that contains them); reference-type objects live on the garbage-collected heap. **Boxing** converts a value type to `object` (allocates and copies); **unboxing** copies it back: avoid it in hot loops (non-generic collections box; `List<int>` does not).

### 3.2 Built-in numeric types

| Type | Size | Range | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `sbyte`, `byte` | 8 bits | -128..127, 0..255 | |
| `short`, `ushort` | 16 bits | ±32,767, 0..65,535 | |
| `int` | 32 bits | -2,147,483,648 .. 2,147,483,647 | the default integer |
| `uint` | 32 bits | 0 .. 4,294,967,295 | |
| `long` | 64 bits | about ±9.2 × 10¹⁸ | use for sums and products |
| `ulong` | 64 bits | 0 .. 1.8 × 10¹⁹ | |
| `float` | 32 bits | ~7 digits | |
| `double` | 64 bits | ~15-16 digits | default for decimals |
| `decimal` | 128 bits | 28-29 digits, exact base-10 | money |
| `char` | 16 bits | one UTF-16 unit | behaves like a number |
| `bool` | 1 byte | `true`/`false` | |
| `BigInteger` | unlimited | `System.Numerics` | exact big integers |
| `nint`, `nuint` | native size | | |

Literals: `1_000_000`, `123L`, `1.5f`, `1.5m`, `'a'`, `0xFF`, `0b1010`. `var x = 5;` infers `int`. Locals must be **definitely assigned** before use. Fields and array elements start at zero/false/`null`.

### 3.3 Conversions
* **Implicit** (widening, lossless): `int` to `long` to `double`.
* **Explicit** (narrowing, may lose data): a cast `(int)3.9` is `3` (truncation); `(byte)300` is `44` (wraps).
* `int` arithmetic is done in `int` even when assigned to a `long`: `long x = a * b;` multiplies as `int` first. Cast first: `(long)a * b`.
* `Convert.ToInt32`, `int.Parse`, `int.TryParse(s, out v)` convert text; `ToString()` formats.

### 3.4 Overflow
Integer arithmetic **wraps around silently** in the default **unchecked** context: `int.MaxValue + 1 == int.MinValue`. Use `checked { ... }` (or the `checked(expr)` operator, or the project setting) to throw `OverflowException`, which is excellent while testing. Constant expressions that overflow are compile errors. Division by zero throws `DivideByZeroException` for integers and gives `Infinity` or `NaN` for floating point. Integer division truncates toward zero and `%` keeps the dividend's sign (`-7 / 2 == -3`, `-7 % 3 == -1`); a non-negative modulo is `((a % m) + m) % m`. Floating point is IEEE 754: `0.1 + 0.2 != 0.3`, so compare with a tolerance or use `decimal`. `int.MinValue` has no positive counterpart: `Math.Abs(int.MinValue)` throws.
Overflow, division, modulo, BigInteger and checked

## 4. Operators and control flow

| Group | Operators | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Arithmetic | `+ - * / %` | `/` on ints truncates |
| Comparison | `== != < <= > >=` | |
| Logical | `&& \|\| !` | short-circuit; `&` and `\|` on bools do not short-circuit |
| Bitwise | `& \| ^ ~ << >> >>>` | `>>>` unsigned shift (C# 11) |
| Null operators | `?.` (null-conditional), `??` (coalescing), `??=` | `name?.Length ?? 0` |
| Conditional | `c ? a : b` | |
| Pattern matching | `x is int n`, `switch` expressions | |

**Conditionals:** `if / else`, `switch` statement or switch expression (`x switch { 1 => "a", _ => "b" }`). **Loops:** `for`, `foreach (var x in items)`, `while`, `do/while`, `break`, `continue`, `goto`. You cannot modify a collection while enumerating it with `foreach` (`InvalidOperationException`). **Counting the cost:** one loop over n is O(n), nested loops O(n²), halving the range O(log n); LINQ calls inside loops can hide O(n) work (`list.Contains`, `Count()`, `Max()` on an enumerable).

## 5. Methods, parameters and references

Methods have a return type, name and parameters; local functions can be declared inside other code (mark `static` to forbid capturing variables). Features: optional parameters, named arguments (`Foo(k: 3)`), expression-bodied members (`int Sq(int x) => x * x;`), tuples to return several values (`(int Lo, int Hi) Range()`), and `params int[] xs`.

### 5.1 How arguments are passed
By default **everything is passed by value**: a copy of the variable. For a value type that is a copy of the data; for a reference type it is a copy of the **reference**, so the method can mutate the shared object but cannot make the caller's variable point elsewhere. The keywords change this: **`ref`** passes the variable itself (the callee may read and reassign it), **`out`** is a return value the callee must assign, and **`in`** passes by read-only reference (avoids copying a big struct). The program below shows each, together with class versus struct, boxing, string equality and nullable value types; predict the output first.
Value versus reference types, ref and out, boxing, string equality and nullable ints

### 5.2 Recursion
Each call uses a stack frame; the default 1 MB stack gives roughly 10⁴ to 10⁵ frames before `StackOverflowException` (which cannot be caught and ends the process). Convert very deep recursion to a loop with an explicit `Stack<T>`. Memoise with a `Dictionary` or an array.

## 6. Strings in depth

`string` is an **immutable** reference type holding UTF-16 code units. Every "change" creates a new string, so appending in a loop is O(n²); use `StringBuilder` (amortised O(1) per append). Literals are **interned** (equal literals share one object). Unlike Java, `==` on strings compares **content**; `ReferenceEquals` compares identity. Strings can be indexed (`s[i]` is a `char`), sliced with ranges (`s[1..4]`, C# 8), and interpolated (`$"n={n}"`).

| Operation | Code | Time | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Length | `s.Length` | O(1) | |
| Index | `s[i]` | O(1) | `IndexOutOfRangeException` if invalid |
| Substring | `s.Substring(a, len)`, `s[a..b]` | O(len) | copies |
| Concatenate | `s + t`, `string.Concat` | O(n + m) | new string |
| Join | `string.Join(",", parts)` | O(total) | |
| Compare | `s == t`, `string.CompareOrdinal` | O(min(n, m)) | `==` is ordinal and case sensitive |
| Search | `IndexOf`, `Contains`, `StartsWith` | O(n·m) worst | culture-sensitive by default for some overloads: prefer `StringComparison.Ordinal` |
| Split | `s.Split(' ')` | O(n) | allocates an array |
| Reverse | `new string(s.Reverse().ToArray())` | O(n) | LINQ |
| `StringBuilder.Append` | | amortised O(1) | `Insert(0, ..)` is O(n) |
| Space | | O(n) | 2 bytes per `char` plus overhead |

`char` arithmetic: `c - 'a'` is 0..25, `c - '0'` a digit; `char.IsDigit`, `IsLetter`, `ToUpper`. A letter-frequency table is an `int[26]`: O(1) update, 26 ints.
Strings, StringBuilder and a counting array

## 7. Arrays and `List<T>` in depth

### 7.1 Arrays
`int[] a = new int[n];` allocates `n` zero-initialised ints in one contiguous block: `a[i]` is O(1) and bounds-checked (`IndexOutOfRangeException`), `a.Length` is the length. Arrays are **reference types**, so `int[] b = a;` aliases; `a.Clone()` or `a[..]` makes a **shallow** copy. **Rectangular** `int[,]` allocates one block of `r × c`; **jagged** `int[][]` is an array of row arrays (each row allocated separately, rows may differ in length; usually the faster and more flexible choice). Static helpers in `Array`: `Sort`, `Fill`, `Reverse`, `IndexOf`, `BinarySearch`, `Copy`, `Resize`.

### 7.2 `List<T>`
A `List<T>` wraps an array that **doubles** when full (copying the elements, O(n) for that one `Add`), so `Add` is **amortised O(1)**.

| Operation | Time | Space | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `list[i]` get/set | O(1) | O(1) | |
| `Add(x)` | amortised O(1), worst O(n) | O(1) amortised | |
| `Insert(i, x)` | O(n) | O(1) | shifts the tail |
| `RemoveAt(i)` | O(n) | O(1) | `RemoveAt(Count - 1)` is O(1) |
| `Remove(x)`, `Contains(x)`, `IndexOf(x)` | O(n) | O(1) | linear scan with `Equals` |
| `Count` | O(1) | O(1) | |
| `Sort()` | O(n log n) | O(log n) | introsort, **not stable** |
| `BinarySearch` | O(log n) | O(1) | sorted input; returns `~insertionPoint` if absent |
| `Reverse()` | O(n) | O(1) | |
| `ToArray()`, copy | O(n) | O(n) | |
| Whole structure | | O(n) | up to 2× capacity |

`List<T>` of a value type stores the values contiguously (no boxing). Set `capacity` in the constructor when you know the size. Do not add or remove while iterating with `foreach`.
Arrays, rectangular and jagged grids, List<T> and tuples

## 8. `Dictionary`, `HashSet` and sorted collections in depth

### 8.1 How `Dictionary<K,V>` works
A `Dictionary` is a **hash table with separate chaining stored in arrays**: a `buckets` array of indexes plus an `entries` array holding key, value, hash and a `next` index for collisions. A key's `GetHashCode()` picks the bucket; `Equals` confirms the match. When the entries array fills, the table **resizes to the next prime** at least double the size and rehashes (O(n), amortised away). Insert, lookup and delete are **O(1) on average**, O(n) in the worst case with terrible hashes. Iteration follows the entries array (usually insertion order if nothing was removed, but **not guaranteed**).

**Keys** need a consistent `Equals` and `GetHashCode`. Strings, numbers, `record`s, value tuples and enums have value-based equality; **arrays and plain classes use reference equality** unless you override or supply an `IEqualityComparer`. The indexer `d[k]` **throws** `KeyNotFoundException` if missing: use `TryGetValue`, `ContainsKey`, `GetValueOrDefault` or `TryAdd`.

`HashSet<T>` is the same table without values. `SortedDictionary<K,V>` and `SortedSet<T>` are **red-black trees**: O(log n) for add/remove/lookup, keys iterate in order, and `SortedSet` offers `Min`, `Max`, `GetViewBetween`. `SortedList<K,V>` is two sorted arrays: O(log n) lookup but **O(n) insertion**.

| Operation | `Dictionary` / `HashSet` | `SortedDictionary` / `SortedSet` | `SortedList` |
|---|---|---|---|
| Add | O(1) avg | O(log n) | O(n) |
| Lookup / `Contains` | O(1) avg | O(log n) | O(log n) |
| Remove | O(1) avg | O(log n) | O(n) |
| Min / max key | O(n) | O(log n) (`Min`/`Max`) | O(1) |
| Iterate | O(n) | O(n) in key order | O(n) in key order |
| Space | O(n) | O(n) node objects | O(n) arrays |
Counting, two-sum, grouping, tuple keys and a sorted set
Value equality for records and tuples, reference equality for arrays, custom comparers

## 9. Stacks, queues, deques and priority queues in depth

| Structure | Class | Operations | Time | Implementation |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Stack (LIFO) | `Stack<T>` | `Push`, `Pop`, `Peek`, `Count` | O(1) amortised each | array that doubles |
| Queue (FIFO) | `Queue<T>` | `Enqueue`, `Dequeue`, `Peek` | O(1) amortised each | **circular array** |
| Deque | `LinkedList<T>` | `AddFirst/Last`, `RemoveFirst/Last` | O(1) each | doubly linked nodes |
| Priority queue | `PriorityQueue<TElement, TPriority>` (.NET 6+) | `Enqueue`, `Dequeue`, `Peek` | O(log n), O(log n), O(1) | **array-based 4-ary min-heap** |

Calling `Pop`/`Dequeue`/`Peek` on an empty collection throws `InvalidOperationException`: check `Count` or use `TryPop`/`TryDequeue`/`TryPeek`. **How the heap works:** a complete tree stored in an array where each parent is ≤ its children (.NET uses four children per node, so the tree is shallower); **Enqueue** appends and sifts up; **Dequeue** moves the last element to the root and sifts down, both O(log n); **Peek** is the root, O(1); **building** from n items (`new PriorityQueue(items)`) is O(n). It is a **min**-heap by priority; for a max-heap pass a comparer that reverses the comparison. There is no decrease-key: enqueue a new entry and ignore stale ones. To keep the k largest of n items use a min-heap of size k: O(n log k) time, O(k) space.

| Operation | `Stack` / `Queue` | `LinkedList` | `PriorityQueue` |
|---|---|---|---|
| Add | O(1)* | O(1) | O(log n) |
| Remove next | O(1) | O(1) | O(log n) |
| Peek | O(1) | O(1) | O(1) |
| Search | O(n) | O(n) | O(n) |
| Build from n items | O(n) | O(n) | O(n) |
| Space | O(n) | O(n) + node objects | O(n) |
Stack, queue, PriorityQueue (min and max) and LinkedList as a deque

## 10. Sorting and searching in depth

`Array.Sort` and `List.Sort` use **introsort** (quicksort with a heapsort fallback and insertion sort for small ranges): O(n log n) worst case, in place, **not stable**. LINQ `OrderBy`/`ThenBy` are **stable** (they use a merge-style approach), O(n log n), and return a new sequence (`ToList()` to materialise). A custom order is a `Comparison<T>` lambda `(a, b) => ...` returning negative, zero or positive, or an `IComparer<T>` via `Comparer<T>.Create`. **Never** subtract in a comparer (`a - b` can overflow): use `a.CompareTo(b)`. `Array.BinarySearch`/`List.BinarySearch` need sorted input, run in O(log n) and return the index, or the **bitwise complement of the insertion point** (`~result`) when absent; they may return any one of several equal elements, so hand-write a `lo`/`hi` loop for first or last position.
Sorting with comparers and LINQ, binary search and intervals

## 11. Classes, structs, records and the object model

* A **class** is a reference type; `new` allocates it on the heap; the garbage collector reclaims it when unreachable. A **struct** is a value type, copied on assignment: good for small immutable data (a point), dangerous when large or mutated through copies. A **record** (C# 9+) is a class (or `record struct`) with **value equality**, `ToString` and `with`-copy generated for you.
* **Equality and hashing:** to use your type as a dictionary or set key, override `Equals` and `GetHashCode` together (or use a `record`).
* **Nullable reference types** (`ListNode?`) let the compiler warn about possible `null` dereferences; `null` access throws `NullReferenceException`.
* **Properties** (`public int X { get; set; }`) replace getters and setters; `readonly` and `init` express immutability.
* **Interfaces and generics:** program to `IList<T>`, `IDictionary<K,V>` or `IEnumerable<T>`; generics are **reified** (the runtime keeps the type argument), unlike Java.
* **Garbage collection:** generations 0, 1 and 2; short-lived objects are cheap. Avoid allocating inside a hot loop (LINQ lambdas, string concatenation, boxing).

### 11.1 Linked lists and trees
A node class holds a value and references; reaching the i-th node costs O(i), inserting after a held node O(1). Check for `null` before dereferencing.
Linked list reversal and tree height

### 11.2 Graphs
Store a graph as an **adjacency list** `List<int>[]` or `List<List<int>>` (O(V + E) space) or `List<(int to, int w)>[]` for weights; an adjacency matrix `int[,]` is O(V²). Breadth-first search with a `Queue<int>` visits each vertex and edge once: **O(V + E) time, O(V) space**, and yields shortest paths in an unweighted graph. For weighted graphs use Dijkstra with `PriorityQueue<int, long>`.
A graph as an array of lists and breadth-first search

## 12. Errors and edge cases

C# reports runtime problems with **exceptions**: `IndexOutOfRangeException`, `KeyNotFoundException`, `NullReferenceException`, `DivideByZeroException`, `InvalidOperationException` (empty `Stack`/`Queue`, `Max()` of an empty sequence), `FormatException`, `OverflowException` (checked only). Use `try / catch / finally` (or `using` for resources). Prefer `TryParse`, `TryGetValue`, `TryPop` patterns over catching, because exceptions are slow when they actually occur.

| Edge case | Typical bug | Defence |
|---|---|---|
| Empty collection | `Max()`, `First()`, `Pop()` throw | check `Count`, or `DefaultIfEmpty`, `FirstOrDefault`, `TryPop` |
| Missing key | `d[k]` throws | `TryGetValue`, `GetValueOrDefault` |
| Integer overflow | wraps silently | `long`, `checked` |
| Null | `NullReferenceException` | nullable reference types, `?.`, `??` |
| Array equality | `==` compares references | `SequenceEqual`, comparer, tuple/record key |
| Modifying while iterating | `InvalidOperationException` | iterate a copy or by index |
| Culture-sensitive string ops | surprising results | `StringComparison.Ordinal` |
TryParse, exceptions, empty-sequence LINQ pitfalls and null operators

## 13. The master complexity cheat sheet

`n` is the number of elements.

| Operation | `T[]` | `List<T>` | `LinkedList<T>` | `Dictionary` / `HashSet` | `SortedDictionary` / `SortedSet` | `Stack` / `Queue` | `PriorityQueue` |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Index | O(1) | O(1) | O(n) | n/a | n/a | n/a | n/a |
| Add at end | n/a | O(1)* | O(1) | O(1)* avg | O(log n) | O(1)* | O(log n) |
| Insert at front | n/a | O(n) | O(1) | n/a | n/a | n/a | n/a |
| Insert in the middle | n/a | O(n) | O(1) at node | n/a | n/a | n/a | n/a |
| Remove at end / next | n/a | O(1) | O(1) | O(1) avg by key | O(log n) | O(1) | O(log n) |
| Remove at front | n/a | O(n) | O(1) | n/a | n/a | queue O(1) | n/a |
| Search by value | O(n) | O(n) | O(n) | O(1) avg by key | O(log n) | O(n) | O(n) |
| Min / max | O(n) | O(n) | O(n) | O(n) | O(log n) | O(n) | O(1) peek |
| Sort | O(n log n) | O(n log n) | n/a | n/a | in order | n/a | n/a |
| Space | O(n) | O(n) | O(n) + nodes | O(n) + entries | O(n) + nodes | O(n) | O(n) |

\* amortised or average.

**What to say in an interview:** "I'll use a `Dictionary<int, int>` from value to index: each `TryGetValue` and insert is O(1) on average, so one pass is O(n) time and O(n) extra space. The brute force is O(n²) time and O(1) space; I'm trading memory for time."

## 14. Pitfalls and idioms checklist

1. `Dictionary` indexer throws on a missing key: use `TryGetValue`.
2. `int` overflow wraps silently: use `long` or `checked`; cast before multiplying.
3. `Array.Sort`/`List.Sort` are not stable; LINQ `OrderBy` is.
4. Never write comparers as `a - b`; use `CompareTo`.
5. `PriorityQueue` dequeues the smallest priority; reverse the comparer for a max-heap.
6. Do not modify a collection inside `foreach` over it.
7. Strings are immutable: use `StringBuilder` in loops.
8. `==` on arrays and most classes compares references; strings and records compare content.
9. A `struct` is copied on assignment; a `class` is shared.
10. `Max()`/`First()`/`Pop()` on empty sources throw: check first.
11. LINQ allocates; prefer loops in hot paths.
12. Use `StringComparison.Ordinal` for deterministic string comparison.
13. Boxing (`object`, non-generic collections) hurts performance.
14. A `StackOverflowException` cannot be caught: avoid deep recursion.

## 15. A reusable solution template
Template: parse, call a pure function, print

## 16. How C# compares with the other languages in this chapter

| Topic | C# | Java | TypeScript | Go |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Value types | `struct`, primitives | primitives only | primitives | structs, arrays |
| Generics | reified | erased | erased | yes (1.18+) |
| Dynamic array | `List<T>` | `ArrayList` | `T[]` | slice |
| Hash map | `Dictionary` | `HashMap` | `Map` | `map` |
| Sorted map | `SortedDictionary` | `TreeMap` | none | none |
| Heap | `PriorityQueue<E,P>` (min) | `PriorityQueue` (min) | write your own | `container/heap` |
| Overflow | wraps (unchecked) | wraps | none (floats) | wraps |

## 17. Practice plan

1. Create a console project with `dotnet new console`, paste each program, run it, and fix anything your SDK version complains about.
2. Solve [Pair With Target Sum](/problems/pair-with-target-sum), [Kth Largest](/problems/kth-largest), [Course Order](/problems/course-order) and [Island Counter](/problems/island-counter) in C#, writing each time and space complexity.
3. Learn `Dictionary`, `HashSet`, `PriorityQueue`, `List.Sort` and LINQ `OrderBy`/`GroupBy`/`Select` by heart.
