blocks:
# Go for Data Structures and Algorithms: a complete guide

This lesson explains Go **as you need it for algorithmic problem solving**: what Go is and how it differs from the other languages here, its types and zero values, integer behaviour, the single `for` loop, functions and pointers, how strings really work (bytes and runes), the inner workings of **slices and maps** (the two types you will use constantly), the standard `sort` and `container/heap` packages, and the **time and space complexity of every operation**.

> **Verification note.** The Java, Python, C++, JavaScript and TypeScript lessons were compiled/type-checked and run before publishing. This machine has no Go toolchain, so every Go program here was written carefully against the standard library (Go 1.21+) but **has not been executed**. Run each at <https://go.dev/play> or with `go run`, and report anything that does not compile.

## 1. What Go is, and why it behaves the way it does

**Go** (Golang) was designed at Google for simple, fast, reliable server software. It is **compiled to native code** (very fast builds), **statically typed**, **garbage collected**, and deliberately **small**: one loop keyword, no classes or inheritance, no exceptions, no operator overloading, no implicit conversions. Concurrency is built in (goroutines and channels), though algorithm problems rarely need it. You compile and run with `go run main.go` or build a binary with `go build`.

| Property | What it means | Consequence |
|---|---|---|
| **Statically typed, no implicit conversions** | Every conversion is written out | `int64(x) * y` needs both operands of the same type |
| **Zero values** | Every variable starts at a defined zero value | No uninitialised memory; a `map` read of a missing key gives the zero value |
| **Garbage collected** | Unreachable memory is reclaimed | No `free`; pointers exist but there is no pointer arithmetic |
| **Composition over inheritance** | `struct`s plus methods plus implicit interfaces | A type satisfies an interface just by having its methods |
| **Errors are values** | Functions return `(result, error)` | Explicit `if err != nil` handling; `panic` is for bugs |
| **Minimal standard data structures** | slice, map, plus `container/heap`, `container/list` | You build stacks, queues and sets from slices and maps |

### Strengths and weaknesses for interviews

| Strengths | Weaknesses |
|---|---|
| Fast to compile and run; simple, readable | No built-in set, stack, queue, deque or sorted map |
| Slices and maps are built into the language | `container/heap` needs interface boilerplate |
| Clear semantics, no hidden magic | Verbose error handling; generics are newer and limited |
| Great for backend and infrastructure roles | Integer overflow wraps silently |

## 2. Program structure and input

Every program is `package main` with a `func main()`; imports are listed in `import ( ... )` and **an unused import or an unused local variable is a compile error**. Names starting with an uppercase letter are exported; lowercase are package-private. Input and output: `fmt.Fscan(reader, &a, &b)` reads whitespace-separated values into variables; wrap `os.Stdin` in a `bufio.Reader` (and `os.Stdout` in a `bufio.Writer`, flushed with `defer out.Flush()`) for speed. Plain `fmt.Println` per line is slow for large output.
Fast input with bufio.Reader and fmt.Fscan

**How it works.** `bufio.NewReader` reads in large chunks; `fmt.Fscan(in, &n, &k)` parses values into the addresses given (`&` takes an address). `make([]int64, n)` creates a slice of `n` zeros. `for i := range nums` iterates the indexes. `defer out.Flush()` schedules the flush to run when `main` returns.

## 3. Data types in depth

### 3.1 Basic types and zero values

| Type | Size | Range | Zero value |
|---|---|---|---|
| `int`, `uint` | 64 bits on 64-bit systems (32 on 32-bit) | ±9.2 × 10¹⁸, 0 .. 1.8 × 10¹⁹ | `0` |
| `int8`, `int16`, `int32`, `int64` | 8/16/32/64 bits | ±127, ±32,767, ±2.1 × 10⁹, ±9.2 × 10¹⁸ | `0` |
| `uint8` (`byte`), `uint16`, `uint32`, `uint64` | 8..64 bits | 0..255, ... | `0` |
| `float32`, `float64` | 32, 64 bits | ~7, ~15-16 digits | `0` |
| `bool` | 1 byte | `true`/`false` | `false` |
| `string` | 16 bytes header | immutable bytes | `""` |
| `rune` (`int32`) | 32 bits | one Unicode code point | `0` |
| pointers, slices, maps, channels, functions, interfaces | | | `nil` |

Because `int` is 64 bits on modern machines, most interview arithmetic fits without special care, but you must still watch `int32` fields and products of two large values. **Untyped constants** (`const MOD = 1_000_000_007`, `1 << 40`) adapt to the type where they are used and are computed with arbitrary precision at compile time; a constant that does not fit its target type is a **compile** error. Declare with `var x int`, `var x = 5`, or the short form `x := 5` (inside functions only).

### 3.2 Overflow and division
**Integer overflow wraps silently** (two's complement): `var a int32 = math.MaxInt32; a++` gives `-2147483648`. There is no exception and no undefined behaviour. Multiply in a wide enough type: `int64(a) * int64(b)`. Integer division **truncates toward zero** (`-7 / 2 == -3`), `%` keeps the dividend's sign (`-7 % 3 == -1`); a non-negative modulo is `((a % m) + m) % m`. **Integer division by zero causes a run-time panic**; floating-point division by zero gives `+Inf` or `NaN`. Floating point is IEEE 754: `0.1 + 0.2 != 0.3`; compare with a tolerance. `math.MaxInt64`, `math.MinInt64`, `math.MaxInt32` are constants; the built-ins `min` and `max` (Go 1.21+) work on ordered types.

### 3.3 No implicit conversion
`var a int = 5; var b int64 = a` is a compile error; write `int64(a)`. Converting a float to an int truncates (`int(3.9) == 3`). `string(65)` gives `"A"` (a code point), not `"65"`; use `strconv.Itoa(65)` for the number text, `strconv.Atoi("65")` to parse (returns `(int, error)`), `strconv.ParseInt`, `strconv.FormatInt(n, 2)` for binary text.

### 3.4 Operators and bits
Arithmetic `+ - * / %`, comparison `== != < <= > >=`, logical `&& || !` (short-circuit), bitwise `& | ^ &^ << >>` (`^x` is bitwise NOT; `&^` is "and not"), assignment `= := += -= ...`, `++` and `--` as **statements** (not expressions). `x & (x - 1)` clears the lowest set bit; `1 << k` is 2ᵏ (use an `int64`/`int` of enough width). There is no ternary operator: write an `if`. Overflow, division and constants in action:

package main

import (
	"fmt"
	"math"
)

func main() {
	var a int32 = math.MaxInt32
	a++
	fmt.Println(a) // -2147483648 (wraps)

	fmt.Println(7/2, -7/2, -7%3) // 3 -3 -1
	m := ((-7 % 3) + 3) % 3
	fmt.Println(m) // 2

	const MOD = 1_000_000_007
	x := int64(123456789) * int64(987654321) % MOD
	fmt.Println(x)

	fmt.Println(math.MaxInt64, math.Sqrt(144), math.Abs(-3.5))
	var inf = math.MaxInt64 // a common "infinity" for minimum searches
	fmt.Println(inf > 1<<40)
}

## 4. Control flow

Go has **only `for`**:

| Form | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `for i := 0; i < n; i++ { }` | the classic counted loop |
| `for cond { }` | a "while" loop |
| `for { }` | infinite loop, leave with `break` or `return` |
| `for i, v := range slice { }` | index and value (use `_` to ignore one) |
| `for k, v := range someMap { }` | key and value, **random order** |
| `for i, r := range str { }` | byte index and **rune** |
| `for i := range 10 { }` | integer range (Go 1.22+) |

`if` takes an optional initialiser (`if v, ok := m[k]; ok { ... }`). `switch` needs no `break` (cases do not fall through; use `fallthrough` explicitly) and can switch on conditions (`switch { case x < 0: ... }`). `break` and `continue` accept labels for nested loops. `defer f()` schedules `f` to run when the surrounding function returns (used for cleanup). **Counting the cost:** one loop over n items is O(n), nested loops O(n²), halving the range O(log n).

## 5. Functions, pointers and references

Functions are declared `func name(a int, b string) (int, error)`; they can return **multiple values**, have **named results**, accept variadic parameters (`xs ...int`), and be passed around as values (closures capture variables). Methods are functions with a receiver: `func (c *Counter) Inc()`.

### 5.1 Everything is passed by value
Go copies every argument. What differs is *what is being copied*:

| Type | What the callee receives | Can it change the caller's data? |
|---|---|---|
| `int`, `float64`, `bool`, `string` | a copy of the value | no |
| **array** `[3]int`, **struct** | a copy of the whole value (O(size)) | no |
| **pointer** `*T` | a copy of the address | **yes**, through the pointer |
| **slice** `[]T` | a copy of the 3-word header (pointer, length, capacity) | **yes** for elements (shared backing array); `append` may or may not be visible |
| **map**, **channel** | a copy of a reference | **yes** |

Methods with a **value receiver** work on a copy; with a **pointer receiver** they can change the original (use pointer receivers when the struct is large or must be mutated). The program shows each case, including the notorious `append` aliasing; predict the output first.

package main

import "fmt"

type Counter struct{ n int }

func (c Counter) IncByValue()    { c.n++ } // receives a COPY of the struct
func (c *Counter) IncByPointer() { c.n++ } // receives a pointer: changes the original

func mutate(arr [3]int, s []int, m map[string]int, p *int) {
	arr[0] = 99     // an array is a value: this changes the local copy
	s[0] = 99       // a slice shares its backing array: the caller sees it
	s = append(s, 7) // may allocate a new array: the caller's slice header is unchanged
	m["k"] = 1      // maps are references: the caller sees it
	*p = 42         // through a pointer: the caller sees it
}

func main() {
	arr := [3]int{1, 2, 3}
	s := []int{1, 2, 3}
	m := map[string]int{}
	x := 5
	mutate(arr, s, m, &x)
	fmt.Println(arr[0], s[0], len(s), m["k"], x) // 1 99 3 1 42

	var c Counter
	c.IncByValue()
	c.IncByPointer()
	fmt.Println(c.n) // 1

	a := []int{1, 2, 3, 4}
	b := a[:2]
	b = append(b, 100) // fits in the capacity of a, so it overwrites a[2]!
	fmt.Println(a, b)  // [1 2 100 4] [1 2 100]

	c2 := append([]int(nil), a...) // a safe independent copy
	c2[0] = -1
	fmt.Println(a[0], c2[0]) // 1 -1

	var nilSlice []int
	fmt.Println(nilSlice == nil, len(nilSlice), cap(nilSlice)) // true 0 0
	nilSlice = append(nilSlice, 1)                             // appending to a nil slice works
	fmt.Println(nilSlice)

	var nilMap map[string]int
	fmt.Println(nilMap["x"], len(nilMap)) // 0 0 (reading a nil map is fine; writing panics)

	x1, x2 := [2]int{1, 2}, [2]int{1, 2}
	fmt.Println(x1 == x2) // true (arrays are comparable by value)
}
Value versus pointer receivers, arrays versus slices, aliasing through append, nil slices and maps

### 5.2 Recursion
Goroutine stacks start small and **grow dynamically** up to a large limit (1 GB on 64-bit), so deep recursion is far less dangerous in Go than in Java or Python, but a runaway recursion still ends in a fatal "stack overflow". Memoise with a `map` or a slice.

## 6. Strings, bytes and runes in depth

A Go `string` is an **immutable sequence of bytes**, conventionally UTF-8 text; it is stored as a (pointer, length) pair, so copying a string is O(1) and **`s[a:b]` is O(1)** (it shares memory, no copy). `len(s)` is the number of **bytes**, not characters. `s[i]` is a `byte` (`uint8`). A **rune** is one Unicode code point; `for i, r := range s` decodes UTF-8 and yields `r` as a rune while `i` is the byte offset; `[]rune(s)` converts to a slice of code points (O(n)). For ASCII problems bytes are enough; for Unicode use runes.

Strings are **immutable**, so to modify, convert: `b := []byte(s)` (copy, O(n)), change `b`, then `string(b)` (copy, O(n)). Concatenating with `+` in a loop is O(n²); use `strings.Builder` (amortised O(1) per write) or collect pieces and `strings.Join`.

| Operation | Code | Time | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Length in bytes | `len(s)` | O(1) | |
| Byte at index | `s[i]` | O(1) | panics if out of range |
| Substring | `s[a:b]` | O(1) | shares memory; end exclusive |
| Concatenate | `s + t` | O(n + m) | new string |
| Compare | `s == t`, `s < t` | O(min(n, m)) | byte-wise |
| Search | `strings.Index(s, t)`, `strings.Contains` | O(n·m) worst | |
| Split / join | `strings.Fields`, `strings.Split`, `strings.Join` | O(n) | `Fields` splits on any whitespace |
| To bytes / runes | `[]byte(s)`, `[]rune(s)` | O(n) | copies |
| Build | `strings.Builder.WriteString/WriteByte/WriteRune` | amortised O(1) | |
| Reverse | swap in a `[]byte` or `[]rune` | O(n) | |
| Space | | O(n) | 1 byte per ASCII char |

Letter frequencies use `var cnt [26]int` and `cnt[s[i]-'a']++`: O(1) update, 26 words of memory.
Strings, bytes, a counting array and strings.Builder

## 7. Arrays and slices in depth

### 7.1 Arrays
`[5]int` is a **fixed-length value**: the length is part of the type, assignment and passing **copy all elements**, and `==` compares element by element. Arrays are rarely used directly except for small fixed tables (`[26]int`, `[2]int` coordinates, `[4][2]int` direction pairs).

### 7.2 Slices: how they really work
A **slice** is a small struct of three words: a **pointer** to an element of an underlying array, a **length** and a **capacity**. `make([]int, n)` creates a zeroed slice of length and capacity `n`; `make([]int, 0, n)` has length 0 and capacity `n`. Operations:

* `a[i]` is O(1) (bounds-checked: out of range **panics**).
* `a[i:j]` creates a new slice header over the **same** array in O(1): **elements are shared**, so writes through one slice are visible through the other.
* `append(a, x)` writes into the next slot if `len < cap` (O(1), and it may overwrite elements visible to another slice, as the program shows), otherwise it **allocates a new array** (growth: about double while small, then roughly 1.25× for large slices), copies all elements (O(n)) and returns a header pointing at the new array. Growth is geometric, so `append` is **amortised O(1)**. **Always assign the result:** `a = append(a, x)`.
* `copy(dst, src)` copies `min(len(dst), len(src))` elements in O(n).
* A **nil slice** (`var a []int`) has length 0, is safe to `append` to and to `range` over, and equals `nil`.

| Operation | Time | Space | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `a[i]` read/write | O(1) | O(1) | bounds-checked |
| `append(a, x)` | amortised O(1), worst O(n) | O(1) amortised | reassign the result |
| `a[i:j]` | O(1) | O(1) | shares the backing array |
| `copy(dst, src)` | O(n) | O(1) | |
| Pop from the end `a = a[:len(a)-1]` | O(1) | O(1) | the element stays in memory until overwritten |
| Pop from the front `a = a[1:]` | O(1) | O(1) | the slice shrinks from the left; the memory is not freed |
| Insert in the middle | O(n) | O(1) | `append(a[:i], append([]int{x}, a[i:]...)...)` or `slices.Insert` |
| Delete in the middle | O(n) | O(1) | `append(a[:i], a[i+1:]...)` or `slices.Delete` |
| Search | O(n) | O(1) | `slices.Index`, `slices.Contains` (Go 1.21+) |
| Sort | O(n log n) | O(log n) | `sort.Ints`, `slices.Sort` |
| Full copy | O(n) | O(n) | `append([]int(nil), a...)` or `slices.Clone` |

**2-D slices** are slices of slices: allocate every row, `grid := make([][]int, r)` then `grid[i] = make([]int, c)`: O(r·c) space. **Pitfall:** the same slice reslice-and-append aliasing can corrupt data silently; when in doubt, copy.
Slices: append, sharing, copy, 2-D grids and deletion

## 8. Maps in depth

A `map[K]V` is a **hash table**. It maps a key's hash to buckets and grows (rehashes) as it fills, so insert, lookup and delete are **O(1) on average** and amortised; the exact internal layout has changed between Go versions but the complexity has not. Properties:

* **Iteration order is random** (deliberately): sort the keys if you need an order.
* Reading a **missing key returns the zero value**; use the **comma-ok** form `v, ok := m[k]` to distinguish "absent" from "zero". `m[k]++` works as a counter because a missing key starts at zero.
* **Writing to a nil map panics.** Create maps with `make(map[K]V)` or a literal `map[K]V{}`. Reading a nil map is fine.
* Keys must be **comparable**: numbers, strings, bools, pointers, **arrays and structs of comparable fields**. Slices, maps and functions are **not** valid keys (compile error). So a coordinate key is `[2]int` or a small struct, or an encoded `int`.
* There is **no set type**: use `map[T]struct{}` (the empty struct takes zero bytes) or `map[T]bool`.
* Maps are **references**: passing a map to a function lets the function modify the caller's map.
* Deleting while ranging over a map is allowed for the current key.
* Maps are not safe for concurrent writes.

| Operation | Time | Space | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `m[k] = v` | O(1) avg | O(1) amortised | |
| `v := m[k]`, `v, ok := m[k]` | O(1) avg | O(1) | |
| `delete(m, k)` | O(1) avg | O(1) | no-op if absent |
| `len(m)` | O(1) | O(1) | |
| iterate | O(n + capacity) | O(1) | random order |
| min / max key | O(n) | O(1) | no sorted map built in |
| whole structure | | O(n), a few dozen bytes per entry | |

For ordered operations (nearest key, sorted iteration) Go has no tree: keep a sorted slice with `sort.Search` (O(log n) find, O(n) insert) or implement a balanced tree.
Counting, two-sum, grouping, sorted iteration and a set of arrays
Struct and array keys, a set from map[T]struct{}, comma-ok lookups and delete

## 9. Stacks, queues, deques and heaps in depth

Go has no stack or queue types; slices do the job.

| Structure | Implementation | Operations | Time |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Stack** | slice: `st = append(st, x)`; top `st[len(st)-1]`; pop `st = st[:len(st)-1]` | push, pop, peek | O(1) each |
| **Queue** | slice plus a head index: `q[head]`, `head++`; or `q = q[1:]` | enqueue, dequeue | O(1) each (memory is released only when the slice is reallocated) |
| **Deque** | `container/list` (doubly linked) or a circular buffer | both ends | O(1) each |
| **Priority queue** | `container/heap` over your slice type | `heap.Push`, `heap.Pop`, `h[0]` | O(log n), O(log n), O(1) |

**How `container/heap` works.** You define a type (often `type IntHeap []int`) implementing `Len`, `Less`, `Swap`, plus `Push(x any)` and `Pop() any` (these two only **append and remove the last element**). You then call **`heap.Push(h, x)`** and **`heap.Pop(h)`**, which call your methods and restore the heap order by sifting up or down (≤ log n swaps); **`heap.Init(h)`** builds a heap from existing data in **O(n)**; **`heap.Fix(h, i)`** repairs one element in O(log n), which gives you a *decrease-key*. The root is `h[0]`. `Less(i, j)` decides the order: `h[i] < h[j]` gives a **min**-heap; flip it for a max-heap. A heap of structs ordered by a field is the standard Dijkstra queue.

| Operation | stack / queue (slice) | `container/list` | `container/heap` |
|---|---|---|---|
| Add | O(1) amortised | O(1) | O(log n) |
| Remove next | O(1) | O(1) | O(log n) |
| Peek | O(1) | O(1) | O(1) |
| Search | O(n) | O(n) | O(n) |
| Build from n items | O(n) | O(n) | O(n) (`heap.Init`) |
| Space | O(n) | O(n) + node objects | O(n) |
Stack and queue on slices, container/heap and container/list

## 10. Sorting and searching in depth

The `sort` package sorts **in place**: `sort.Ints`, `sort.Strings`, `sort.Float64s`, and `sort.Slice(s, func(i, j int) bool { ... })` for any slice (the function says whether element `i` must come **before** `j`). `sort.Slice` is **not stable**; `sort.SliceStable` is, and both are O(n log n). Go 1.21+ adds `slices.Sort`, `slices.SortFunc`, `slices.BinarySearch` and the `cmp` package (`cmp.Compare`). The comparison must be a consistent *strict* ordering (`<`, not `<=`). `sort.Search(n, f)` does a binary search for the **smallest index where `f(i)` is true** (requires monotone `f`), O(log n); `sort.SearchInts(a, x)` is the first index with `a[i] >= x`.
sort.Slice with multiple keys, SearchInts and sort.Search

## 11. Structs, methods, pointers and interfaces

A `struct` groups fields; methods attach to any named type. **Pointers** (`*T`, address-of `&x`, dereference `*p`) let you share and mutate; a **nil pointer** dereference panics, so test `p != nil`. There is no pointer arithmetic. `new(T)` and `&T{...}` allocate; **escape analysis** decides whether a value lives on the stack or the heap (you do not choose). **Interfaces** are satisfied **implicitly**: a type that has the methods of `sort.Interface` or `heap.Interface` *is* one. The empty interface `any` holds any value (needs a type assertion to use). **Generics** (Go 1.18+) let you write `func Max[T cmp.Ordered](a, b T) T`.

**Garbage collection** reclaims unreachable memory concurrently; avoid keeping huge slices alive through small sub-slices (a `s[:10]` of a million-element slice still pins the whole array: copy what you need).

### 11.1 Linked lists and trees
Nodes are structs with pointer fields (`Next *ListNode`, `Left, Right *TreeNode`); a `nil` pointer ends a chain. Reaching the i-th node costs O(i); inserting after a held node is O(1); recursion depth equals tree height.
Linked list reversal and tree height with pointers

### 11.2 Graphs
Store a graph as an **adjacency list** `[][]int` (O(V + E) space) or `[][]Edge` for weights; an adjacency matrix `[][]int` is O(V²). Breadth-first search with a slice-queue and a head index visits each vertex and edge once: **O(V + E) time, O(V) space**, shortest paths in an unweighted graph. Dijkstra uses `container/heap` for **O((V + E) log V)**.
A graph as a slice of slices and breadth-first search with a head index

## 12. Errors, panics and edge cases

Go does **not** use exceptions for ordinary failures. Functions return an `error` as the last result; callers check it: `v, err := strconv.Atoi(s); if err != nil { ... }`. Create errors with `errors.New("...")` or `fmt.Errorf("...: %w", err)` (the `%w` verb **wraps** an error, and `errors.Is(err, target)` / `errors.As` inspect the chain). A **`panic`** is for bugs: out-of-range index, nil map write, nil pointer dereference, integer divide by zero, failed type assertion. A panic unwinds the stack running `defer`red functions; `recover()` inside a deferred function stops it. In algorithm code you mostly **prevent** panics by checking edge cases:

| Edge case | Typical bug | Defence |
|---|---|---|
| Empty slice | `a[0]` panics | check `len(a) == 0` |
| Index out of range | `a[len(a)]` panics | validate indexes; loop with `range` |
| Missing map key | zero value mistaken for a real value | comma-ok `v, ok := m[k]` |
| Write to nil map | panic | `make` the map |
| Overflow | wraps silently | `int64`, check before multiplying |
| `append` aliasing | unexpected overwrite | copy with `slices.Clone` |
| Integer division by zero | panic | check the divisor |
| Unused variable / import | compile error | delete it or use `_` |
Errors as values, wrapping, panic and recover, bounds panics and empty-input handling

## 13. The master complexity cheat sheet

`n` is the number of elements.

| Operation | slice | array | `map` | `container/list` | `container/heap` | `string` |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Access by index / key | O(1) | O(1) | O(1) avg | O(n) | root `h[0]` O(1) | O(1) (byte) |
| Append / push at end | O(1)* | n/a | O(1)* insert | O(1) | O(log n) | O(n) (`+`) |
| Pop from end | O(1) | n/a | n/a | O(1) | O(log n) | n/a |
| Pop from front | O(1) (re-slice) | n/a | n/a | O(1) | n/a | O(1) (re-slice) |
| Insert / delete in the middle | O(n) | n/a | O(1) avg by key | O(1) at element | O(log n) (`heap.Fix`/`Remove`) | O(n) |
| Search by value | O(n) | O(n) | O(1) avg by key | O(n) | O(n) | O(n·m) |
| Min / max | O(n) | O(n) | O(n) | O(n) | O(1) | O(n) |
| Sort | O(n log n) | O(n log n) | n/a | n/a | n/a | via `[]byte` |
| Copy | O(n) | O(n) | O(n) | O(n) | O(n) | O(1) (header) |
| Space | O(n) | O(n) | O(n), heavier | O(n) + nodes | O(n) | O(n) |

\* amortised or average.

**What to say in an interview:** "I'll keep a `map[int]int` from value to index. Each lookup and insert is O(1) on average, so one pass is O(n) time with O(n) extra space. The brute force is O(n²) time and O(1) space; I'm trading memory for time."

## 14. Pitfalls and idioms checklist

1. Always assign the result of `append`: `a = append(a, x)`.
2. Re-slicing **shares memory**; use `copy` / `slices.Clone` for independence.
3. Reading a missing map key returns the zero value; use comma-ok.
4. Writing to a **nil map** panics; `make` it.
5. Map iteration order is random; sort keys when order matters.
6. Integer overflow wraps silently; `int` is 64-bit but `int32` is not.
7. `len(s)` counts **bytes**; use `[]rune(s)` for characters.
8. There are no implicit conversions: write `int64(x)`.
9. Unused variables and imports do not compile.
10. Use pointer receivers when a method must modify the struct.
11. Slices, maps and functions cannot be map keys; use arrays or structs.
12. Call `heap.Push`/`heap.Pop`, not the type's own `Push`/`Pop` methods.
13. `for _, v := range s` gives a **copy** of each element: modify via the index (`s[i].x = ...`).
14. A panic crashes the program unless recovered: check bounds and divisors.

## 15. A reusable solution template
Template: parse, call a pure function, print

## 16. How Go compares with the other languages in this chapter

| Topic | Go | Java | C++ | Python |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Dynamic array | slice | `ArrayList` | `vector` | `list` |
| Hash map | `map` | `HashMap` | `unordered_map` | `dict` |
| Set | `map[T]struct{}` | `HashSet` | `unordered_set` | `set` |
| Sorted map | none | `TreeMap` | `map` | none |
| Heap | `container/heap` | `PriorityQueue` | `priority_queue` | `heapq` |
| Errors | return values | exceptions | exceptions / UB | exceptions |
| Overflow | wraps | wraps | UB (signed) | none |
| Missing key | zero value | `null` | inserts default | `KeyError` |

## 17. Practice plan

1. Run every program on the Go Playground, change the inputs, and explain each output.
2. Solve [Pair With Target Sum](/problems/pair-with-target-sum), [Kth Largest](/problems/kth-largest), [Cheapest Route](/problems/cheapest-route) and [Shortest Maze Path](/problems/shortest-maze-path) in Go, writing each time and space complexity; the third needs `container/heap`.
3. Practise the heap boilerplate until you can write it from memory; it is the part of Go interviews people forget.

# JavaScript for Data Structures and Algorithms: a complete guide

This lesson explains JavaScript **as you need it for algorithmic problem solving**: what it is and how the engine runs it, every primitive type and its quirks, equality and coercion, scope and functions, strings, arrays, `Map` and `Set`, and how to build the structures the language lacks (a heap, a deque) with the **time and space complexity of every operation**. The programs were run on Node.js.

## 1. What JavaScript is, and why it behaves the way it does

**JavaScript** was created for web browsers and now also runs servers (**Node.js**), mobile apps and tools. A **JavaScript engine** (V8 in Chrome and Node, SpiderMonkey in Firefox, JavaScriptCore in Safari) parses your code, starts running it in an interpreter and then **JIT-compiles** hot functions to machine code, so modern JavaScript is fast for such a dynamic language, typically within a small factor of Java. A program runs on a **single thread** with an **event loop** for asynchronous work; for algorithm problems you only need the synchronous part.

| Property | What it means | Consequence |
|---|---|---|
| **Dynamically typed** | Values have types, variables do not | Flexible, but type errors show up at run time; TypeScript adds static types |
| **One `number` type** | Every ordinary number is a 64-bit float | Integers are exact only up to 2⁵³ - 1; use `BigInt` beyond |
| **Reference semantics for objects** | Arrays and objects are references | Assignment aliases; copies must be explicit |
| **Weak and surprising coercion** | `==`, `+` convert types implicitly | Always use `===` and explicit conversions |
| **Garbage collected** | Unreachable objects are freed | No manual memory management |
| **Thin standard library** | No heap, deque or tree map built in | You write small helper classes |

### Strengths and weaknesses for interviews

| Strengths | Weaknesses |
|---|---|
| Common in web, full-stack and Node roles | No priority queue, deque or sorted map in the language |
| Concise array methods (`map`, `filter`, `reduce`) | Default `sort()` compares as **strings** |
| `Map` and `Set` with insertion order | Precision loss above 2⁵³ - 1 |
| `BigInt` for exact huge integers | Type coercion surprises |

## 2. Program structure and input

A script runs top to bottom; there is no `main`. Statements end with `;` (optional but recommended). Modules use `import`/`export` (or `require` in classic Node). In Node you read all of standard input with `require("fs").readFileSync(0, "utf8")` (file descriptor 0). `console.log` prints; each call is a system call, so for many lines build an array and `join("\n")` once.
Read all tokens, convert to numbers

**How it works.** `readFileSync(0, "utf8")` returns the whole input as one string; `split(/\s+/)` splits on any whitespace (the regular expression matches runs of spaces and newlines); `filter(Boolean)` removes empty strings (a leading or trailing separator creates one); `map(Number)` converts each token to a number. Total cost is O(length of the input), once.

## 3. Data types in depth

### 3.1 The seven primitive types and objects

| Type | Examples | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `number` | `42`, `3.14`, `NaN`, `Infinity`, `-0` | 64-bit IEEE 754 float; the only number type |
| `bigint` | `123n`, `2n ** 100n` | arbitrary-precision integers; do not mix with `number` |
| `string` | `"abc"`, `'abc'`, `` `abc ${x}` `` | immutable UTF-16 text |
| `boolean` | `true`, `false` | |
| `undefined` | a variable never assigned | "no value yet" |
| `null` | explicit "no object" | `typeof null` is `"object"` (a historic bug) |
| `symbol` | `Symbol("id")` | unique identifiers; rare in algorithms |
| **objects** | `{}`, `[]`, functions, `Map`, `Set`, `Date` | everything else; compared **by reference** |

`typeof` reports the kind: `"number"`, `"string"`, `"boolean"`, `"undefined"`, `"object"` (also for arrays and null), `"function"`. Use `Array.isArray(x)` to detect arrays.

### 3.2 Numbers: floats, integers and precision
All numbers are 64-bit doubles: 1 sign bit, 11 exponent bits, 52 fraction bits. Consequences:

* **Integers are exact only up to `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER` = 2⁵³ - 1 = 9,007,199,254,740,991.** Above that, neighbouring integers collapse: `2 ** 53 === 2 ** 53 + 1` is `true`. Sums or products of large values silently lose precision. Use **`BigInt`** (`123n`, `BigInt(x)`) for exact big integers; mix types only after converting.
* Decimals are approximate: `0.1 + 0.2 === 0.3` is `false`. Compare with a tolerance (`Math.abs(a - b) < 1e-9`).
* Special values: `Infinity`, `-Infinity`, `NaN` ("not a number"). `NaN !== NaN`; test with `Number.isNaN(x)`. Division by zero **does not throw**: `1 / 0 === Infinity`, `0 / 0` is `NaN`.
* There is no integer division: use `Math.floor(a / b)` (for non-negative) or `Math.trunc` (rounds toward zero). `%` keeps the sign of the dividend, so `-7 % 3 === -1`; a non-negative modulo is `((a % m) + m) % m`.
* **Bitwise operators convert to 32-bit signed integers**: `1 << 31` is negative, `2 ** 32 | 0` is `0`. Use them only for values under 2³¹; for larger values use arithmetic or `BigInt`.
* Conversions: `Number("42")`, `Number("")` is **0**, `Number("12px")` is `NaN`, `parseInt("12px", 10)` is 12 (always pass the radix), `String(12)`, `(12).toString(2)` gives binary text, `Math.round`, `Math.floor`, `Math.ceil`.

### 3.3 Truthiness, equality and coercion
**Falsy values** (treated as false in conditions): `false`, `0`, `-0`, `0n`, `""`, `null`, `undefined`, `NaN`. Everything else is truthy, including `"0"`, `[]` and `{}`. `if (!arr.length)` is the right empty test for an array; `if (!arr)` is not.

`==` **coerces** types and gives surprising results (`"" == 0`, `"0" == false`, `null == undefined` are all true); `===` compares without coercion. **Use `===` and `!==` always.** `Object.is(a, b)` is like `===` but treats `NaN` as equal to itself and distinguishes `0` from `-0`. Objects and arrays are equal only if they are the **same object**: `[1] === [1]` is `false`.

### 3.4 Variables and scope
`const` (cannot be rebound; the object it names can still be mutated), `let` (block scoped) and the legacy `var` (function scoped and hoisted, a source of bugs). Prefer `const`, then `let`. Declarations are **hoisted**: a `let`/`const` exists from the start of its block but cannot be used before its line (the "temporal dead zone"). The program below also shows the classic `var` closure bug.

console.log(0.1 + 0.2 === 0.3);                // false (floating point)
console.log(Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER + 2);        // 9007199254740992 (precision lost)
console.log(2n ** 100n);                         // exact big integer
console.log(Math.floor(7 / 2), Math.trunc(-7 / 2), -7 % 3);   // 3 -3 -1
console.log(((-7 % 3) + 3) % 3);                 // 2
console.log("1" == 1, "1" === 1);                // true false
console.log(1 << 31, 2 ** 31 | 0);               // -2147483648 -2147483648
const MOD = 1_000_000_007n;
console.log(123456789n * 987654321n % MOD);     // BigInt modular product
Pass by sharing, equality traps, typeof, copies and var versus let closures

## 4. Operators and control flow

| Group | Operators | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Arithmetic | `+ - * / % **` | `+` also concatenates strings: `1 + "2"` is `"12"`, `"3" * "4"` is `12` |
| Comparison | `=== !== < <= > >=` | `"10" < "9"` is `true` (string comparison); compare numbers as numbers |
| Logical | `&& \|\| !` and `??` | `a \|\| b` returns `b` for any falsy `a`; **`a ?? b` only for `null`/`undefined`**, so `0 ?? 5` is `0` |
| Optional chaining | `a?.b`, `a?.[i]`, `f?.()` | stops with `undefined` if `a` is nullish |
| Bitwise | `& \| ^ ~ << >> >>>` | 32-bit |
| Spread / rest | `[...a]`, `{...o}`, `(...args)` | copies one level; arguments |
| Destructuring | `const [a, b] = pair`, `const {x, y} = pt` | `[a, b] = [b, a]` swaps |

**Control flow.** `if / else if / else`, `switch` (strict comparison, falls through without `break`), `for (init; cond; step)`, `for (const x of iterable)` (values, for arrays, strings, Maps, Sets), `for (const k in obj)` (keys; avoid on arrays), `while`, `do while`, `break`, `continue`, labels. Array methods `forEach`, `map`, `filter`, `reduce`, `some`, `every`, `find`, `findIndex` take callbacks; they are O(n) each and cannot `break` early (use a loop when you need to stop).

**Counting the cost.** A loop over n items is O(n). Be careful with *hidden* linear work inside loops: `arr.includes(x)`, `arr.indexOf(x)`, `arr.shift()`, `arr.slice()` and `[...arr]` are O(n) each, so using them inside a loop makes it O(n²). Replace membership tests with a `Set`.

## 5. Functions in depth

Functions are values. Forms: declaration `function f(a, b) {}` (hoisted), expression `const f = function () {}`, **arrow** `(a, b) => a + b` (shorter, no own `this`). Features: default parameters `(a, b = 1)`, rest `...args`, destructured parameters. **Closures** capture variables from the surrounding scope (the `for (var ...)` example above is a closure bug). A function that does not `return` gives `undefined`. Arguments are **passed by sharing**: the parameter gets a copy of the value, which for objects is a reference to the same object, so the callee can mutate it but cannot rebind the caller's variable (the same rule as Java and Python). The recursion limit is roughly 10⁴ frames (`RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded`); convert deep recursion to a loop with an explicit stack. Memoise with a `Map`.

## 6. Strings in depth

A string is an **immutable** sequence of UTF-16 code units. `s[0] = "x"` silently does nothing. Characters outside the basic plane (many emoji) are two code units, which matters for `length` and indexing on Unicode text. `s[i]` returns a one-character *string* (there is no `char`).

| Operation | Code | Time | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Length | `s.length` | O(1) | property, not a method |
| Index | `s[i]`, `s.at(-1)`, `s.charAt(i)` | O(1) | out of range gives `undefined` / `""` |
| Char code / back | `s.charCodeAt(i)`, `String.fromCharCode(97)` | O(1) | letter index: `s.charCodeAt(i) - 97` |
| Substring | `s.slice(a, b)` | O(b - a) (engines may share memory) | end exclusive; negative counts from the end |
| Concatenate | `s + t`, `` `${s}${t}` `` | amortised cheap | engines build "ropes"; still avoid in huge nested loops |
| Join | `parts.join("")` | O(total) | the safe way to build large strings |
| Compare | `s === t`, `s < t` | O(min(n, m)) | `localeCompare` for locale order |
| Search | `s.indexOf(t)`, `s.includes(t)` | O(n·m) worst | |
| Split | `s.split(" ")`, `[...s]` | O(n) | `[...s]` iterates code points |
| Reverse | `[...s].reverse().join("")` | O(n) | |
| Case, trim | `toLowerCase`, `trim` | O(n) | |
| Space | | O(n) | 1 or 2 bytes per code unit in the engine |

`Array.from("abc")` or `[..."abc"]` gives characters; `for (const c of s)` iterates code points. Template literals `` `n=${n}` `` interpolate values.

## 7. Arrays in depth

A JavaScript array is a **dynamic, resizable list** of values (it is actually an object with special behaviour). Engines such as V8 store arrays of small integers, of doubles, or of mixed values in contiguous memory with **specialised element kinds**, and switch representation if you add a different type, so keeping an array **homogeneous** and **dense** (no holes, filled in order) keeps it fast. `a[i]` is O(1). Appending grows the backing store geometrically, so `push` is **amortised O(1)**. For numeric work where speed matters use **typed arrays**: `new Int32Array(n)`, `new Float64Array(n)` are fixed-length, zero-filled, contiguous and allocation-light.

| Operation | Code | Time | Space | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Read / write | `a[i]`, `a[i] = x` | O(1) | O(1) | writing past the end creates holes: avoid |
| Append / pop at end | `push`, `pop` | amortised O(1) / O(1) | O(1) | |
| Add / remove at front | `unshift`, `shift` | **O(n)** | O(1) | shifts all elements (engines optimise small cases, never rely on it) |
| Insert / delete in the middle | `splice(i, k, ...)` | O(n) | O(k) | |
| Slice / copy | `slice`, `[...a]`, `Array.from(a)` | O(n) | O(n) | shallow |
| Concatenate | `a.concat(b)`, `[...a, ...b]` | O(n + m) | O(n + m) | |
| Search | `indexOf`, `includes`, `find` | O(n) | O(1) | `includes` treats `NaN` as equal |
| Sort | `sort(cmp)` | O(n log n) | O(n) | stable (TimSort in V8) |
| Reverse | `reverse()` | O(n) | O(1) | in place |
| `map` / `filter` / `reduce` | | O(n) | O(n) / O(n) / O(1) | `map`/`filter` allocate a new array |
| Min / max | `Math.max(...a)` | O(n) | O(n) args | **spread of ~10⁵+ items can overflow the call stack**: use `reduce` or a loop |
| Fill | `new Array(n).fill(0)` | O(n) | O(n) | |
| Length | `a.length` | O(1) | | assigning a smaller length truncates |

**Sorting trap:** `[10, 9, 1].sort()` returns `[1, 10, 9]`, because the default comparison converts elements to **strings**. Always pass `(x, y) => x - y` for numbers.

**Copy traps:** `const b = a` aliases; `[...a]` is a **shallow** copy (rows of a 2-D array are shared); `structuredClone(a)` deep-copies. `new Array(r).fill(new Array(c))` shares **one** row `r` times; build grids with `Array.from({ length: r }, () => new Array(c).fill(0))`. Holes: `new Array(5)` has no elements (`.map` skips them); use `.fill`.
Arrays, the sort trap, 2-D grids and array methods

## 8. `Map` and `Set` in depth

### 8.1 How they work
`Map` and `Set` are **hash tables** that remember **insertion order**. A key's hash chooses a slot; collisions are resolved internally; the table grows when it fills, so insertion is amortised O(1).

* **Keys keep their type** in a `Map` (`1` and `"1"` are different keys) and can be anything, including objects (compared **by identity**). A plain **object** used as a map converts every key to a **string** (so `o[1]` and `o["1"]` are the same), inherits properties such as `toString`, and has no `size`. Prefer `Map` for numeric or non-string keys and for counting; use `Object.create(null)` if you need an object-map without inherited names.
* Equal arrays are **different keys**: encode coordinates as a string (`` `${r},${c}` ``), a number (`r * cols + c`), or `JSON.stringify`.

| Operation | `Map` / `Set` | Plain object as a map |
|---|---|---|
| set / add | O(1) amortised | O(1) average |
| get / has | O(1) average | O(1) average |
| delete | O(1) average | O(1) (`delete o.k` can slow the engine) |
| size | O(1) (`m.size`) | O(n) (`Object.keys(o).length`) |
| iterate | O(n), insertion order | O(n), numeric-like keys first, then insertion order |
| space | O(n) | O(n) |

Methods: `m.set(k, v)`, `m.get(k)`, `m.has(k)`, `m.delete(k)`, `m.size`, iteration with `for (const [k, v] of m)`, `m.keys()`, `m.values()`, `[...m]`; `s.add(x)`, `s.has(x)`, `s.delete(x)`, `[...s]`. Remove duplicates with `[...new Set(a)]` (O(n)). There is **no built-in sorted map or tree set**: keep a sorted array and use binary search, whose insertion is O(n).
Counting, two-sum, grouping and Set of coordinates
Map versus object keys, identity versus value keys, coordinate encoding and an LRU cache

## 9. Stacks, queues, deques and heaps

JavaScript has no dedicated types for these; you build them from arrays and small classes.

| Structure | Implementation | Operations | Time |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Stack** | array: `push`, `pop`, `a.at(-1)` | push, pop, peek | O(1) each |
| **Queue** | array with a **head index**: `q.push(x)`, `q[head++]` | enqueue, dequeue | O(1) each (`shift()` would be O(n)) |
| **Deque** | two pointers over an array, or a doubly linked list | both ends | O(1) each |
| **Heap / priority queue** | a binary heap class over an array | push, pop, peek | O(log n), O(log n), O(1) |
| **Sorted structure** | sorted array + binary search | find, insert | O(log n), O(n) |

**How the heap works.** Store a complete binary tree in an array: element `i` has children `2i + 1` and `2i + 2` and parent `(i - 1) >> 1`. **Push:** append, then *sift up* while smaller than the parent (at most log n swaps). **Pop:** take the root, move the last element to the root, then *sift down* swapping with the smaller child (at most log n swaps). **Peek:** the root, O(1). **Heapify** n items in O(n). Making it a **max**-heap only needs a flipped comparator. Interviewers allowing JavaScript expect you to write this in a few minutes: practise it until it is automatic.

To keep the **k largest** of a stream use a min-heap of size k: O(n log k) time, O(k) space. The **head-index queue** never frees consumed slots; for very long streams periodically `queue = queue.slice(head); head = 0`.
A reusable MinHeap, plus stack and queue

## 10. Sorting, comparators and searching

`Array.prototype.sort` is **stable** (guaranteed since ES2019) and runs in O(n log n). The comparator returns a negative number, zero, or a positive number; combine keys with `||`: `(a, b) => b.age - a.age || a.name.localeCompare(b.name)`. It is safe to subtract numbers here because JavaScript numbers are floats and do not wrap (but subtracting `Infinity` values or `NaN` breaks it). `sort` sorts **in place** and returns the same array; `toSorted()` (newer engines) returns a copy; copy first with `[...a].sort(...)` when you must keep the original.

There is no built-in binary search: write the `lo/hi` loop yourself, for example `lowerBound` (first index with `a[i] >= x`) below. `Array.prototype.toSorted`, `findLast` and `at` exist in modern Node versions.
Multi-key sort, lowerBound and interval sort

## 11. Objects, classes and the memory model

An **object** is a collection of key-value properties; arrays, functions, `Map` and `Set` are objects. Objects live on the **heap** and variables hold **references**. `class` syntax defines constructors and methods; fields are public by default (`#private` fields exist). `this` depends on how a function is called (arrow functions capture the surrounding `this`). Equality and hashing are by **identity** for objects, so equal-looking objects are different keys in a `Map`/`Set`. The engine's **garbage collector** frees objects no longer reachable; a long-lived cache or a closure that holds a big array is the usual "leak". Property access on objects is O(1) average.

### 11.1 Linked lists and trees
A node is a small object or class with references (`next`, `left`, `right`). `null` ends a list; dereferencing `null` throws `TypeError`, so test `node !== null`. Reaching the i-th node of a list is O(i); inserting after a node you hold is O(1). A tree of height h has recursion depth h (up to n for a degenerate tree, which can overflow the stack).
Linked list reversal and tree height

### 11.2 Graphs
Store a graph as an **adjacency list**, an array of arrays (`adj[u]` lists the neighbours of `u`): O(V + E) space. An adjacency matrix is O(V²). Breadth-first search with a head-index queue visits each vertex and edge once: **O(V + E) time, O(V) space**, and gives shortest paths in an unweighted graph.
A graph as an array of arrays and breadth-first search with a head index

## 12. Errors and edge cases

JavaScript signals problems with **exceptions** (`throw new Error("...")`, `try / catch / finally`) and, much more often, with **silent odd values**: `undefined` from a missing index or property, `NaN` from a failed conversion, `Infinity` from division by zero. Most algorithm bugs are silent, so check edge cases deliberately.

| Edge case | Typical bug | Defence |
|---|---|---|
| Empty array | `Math.max(...[])` is `-Infinity`; `a[0]` is `undefined` | `if (a.length === 0) return ...` |
| Missing map key | `m.get(k)` is `undefined`; `undefined + 1` is `NaN` | `m.get(k) ?? 0` |
| Number conversion | `Number("")` is `0`, `Number("12px")` is `NaN` | validate with `Number.isInteger` / `Number.isNaN` |
| Large integers | silent precision loss above 2⁵³ - 1 | `BigInt`, or check `Number.isSafeInteger` |
| `shift()` in a loop | O(n²) | head index |
| `sort()` without comparator | string order | `(x, y) => x - y` |
| Optional values | `null.x` throws `TypeError` | `x?.y`, `x ?? default` |
Number conversion pitfalls, empty-input results, optional chaining and exceptions

## 13. The master complexity cheat sheet

`n` is the number of elements.

| Operation | `Array` | typed array | `Map` / `Set` | object as map | string |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Access by index / key | O(1) | O(1) | O(1) avg (key) | O(1) avg | O(1) |
| Push / pop at end | O(1)* / O(1) | n/a | n/a | n/a | n/a |
| Shift / unshift (front) | **O(n)** | n/a | n/a | n/a | n/a |
| Insert / delete in the middle | O(n) | n/a | O(1) avg (by key) | O(1) avg | O(n) |
| Search by value | O(n) | O(n) | O(1) avg (key) | O(1) avg (key) | O(n·m) |
| Min / max | O(n) | O(n) | O(n) | O(n) | O(n) |
| Sort | O(n log n) | O(n log n) | n/a | n/a | O(n log n) via array |
| Iterate | O(n) | O(n) | O(n) | O(n) | O(n) |
| Copy | O(n) | O(n) | O(n) | O(n) | O(1)-O(n) |
| Space | O(n) | 4/8 bytes per item | O(n), heavier | O(n), heavier | O(n) |

\* amortised or average. **Heap** (your class): push O(log n), pop O(log n), peek O(1).

**What to say in an interview:** "I'll keep a `Map` from value to index. Each lookup and insert is O(1) on average, so one pass is O(n) time and O(n) extra space. The brute force is O(n²) time and O(1) space; I'm trading memory for time."

## 14. Pitfalls and idioms checklist

1. `arr.sort()` without a comparator sorts as strings.
2. Always use `===` and `!==`.
3. Floats are inexact (`0.1 + 0.2 !== 0.3`); integers above 2⁵³ - 1 lose precision: use `BigInt`.
4. `shift()` and `unshift()` are O(n): use a head index.
5. `new Array(n).fill([])` shares one inner array; use `Array.from`.
6. `Math.max(...hugeArray)` can crash the call stack; use a loop or `reduce`.
7. `[...a]` and `slice()` are shallow; use `structuredClone` for deep copies.
8. `Number("")` is `0`; `parseInt("08", 10)`: pass the radix; validate input.
9. Object keys become strings; use `Map` for numeric or object keys.
10. Equal arrays/objects are not equal keys; encode them.
11. `for...in` iterates keys (strings); use `for...of` for values.
12. Bitwise operators truncate to 32 bits.
13. `var` is function scoped: use `let` and `const`.
14. Recursion depth is about 10⁴: use iteration for deep structures.

## 15. A reusable solution template
Template: parse, call a pure function, print

## 16. How JavaScript compares with the other languages in this chapter

| Topic | JavaScript | TypeScript | Python | Java |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Typing | dynamic | static (erased) | dynamic | static |
| Integers | float (exact to 2⁵³) / `BigInt` | same | unlimited | 32/64-bit wrapping |
| Dynamic array | `Array` | `T[]` | `list` | `ArrayList` |
| Hash map | `Map` | `Map<K,V>` | `dict` | `HashMap` |
| Heap | write your own | write your own | `heapq` | `PriorityQueue` |
| Sorted map | none | none | none | `TreeMap` |
| Default sort | string order! | string order! | numeric | n/a |

## 17. Practice plan

1. Re-type the `MinHeap` until you can write it from memory; it unlocks top-k, Dijkstra and scheduling problems.
2. Solve [Pair With Target Sum](/problems/pair-with-target-sum), [Kth Largest](/problems/kth-largest), [Island Counter](/problems/island-counter) and [Shortest Maze Path](/problems/shortest-maze-path) in JavaScript, and write each time and space complexity.
3. Explain aloud why `sort()` needs a comparator, why `shift()` is slow and why `0.1 + 0.2 !== 0.3`: interviewers like these answers.

blocks:
# TypeScript for Data Structures and Algorithms: a complete guide

TypeScript is **JavaScript with a static type system**. Everything in the *JavaScript for DSA* lesson (the engine, numbers, `Array`, `Map`, `Set`, sorting, the missing heap) is still true, because TypeScript is **erased** to plain JavaScript before running. What TypeScript adds is a layer of checking at compile time: it refuses programs that pass a string where a number is expected, forget the `undefined` case, or misspell a field. This lesson explains that type layer in depth and then shows how each data structure looks in typed code, with the **time and space complexity of every operation**. Every program was **type-checked with `tsc --strict`** and run.

## 1. What TypeScript is, and why it behaves the way it does

TypeScript (TS) is a **superset** of JavaScript: every valid JavaScript program is valid TypeScript. The compiler `tsc` (or a faster tool such as `esbuild`, `swc`, or Node's built-in type stripping) checks types and then **removes** them, producing ordinary JavaScript. Types therefore **cost nothing at run time**, and they **disappear at run time**: you cannot ask "is this an `interface Person`?" while the program runs, only inspect real values (`typeof`, `in`, `instanceof`, a tag field).

| Property | What it means | Consequence |
|---|---|---|
| **Static, structural typing** | Types are checked before running; two types are compatible when their *shapes* match | You rarely need to declare that a class "implements" something; matching fields is enough |
| **Gradual** | You can opt out with `any` | `any` switches checking off: avoid it |
| **Erased** | Types are not present at run time | No type-based dispatch; use tagged unions |
| **Same runtime as JavaScript** | Floats, `NaN`, coercion, `sort()` as strings | All JS pitfalls remain |
| **`strict` mode** | A family of checks (`strictNullChecks`, `noImplicitAny`, ...) | Forces you to handle `undefined`/`null` |

### Strengths and weaknesses for interviews

| Strengths | Weaknesses |
|---|---|
| Types document intent and catch bugs before running | Extra syntax; types are only as good as you write them |
| `strict` null checks remove the most common JS runtime error | Same runtime pitfalls as JavaScript |
| Excellent for modelling nodes, edges, results with unions | No built-in heap, deque or sorted map |
| Very common in front-end and Node.js jobs | Generic type errors can be long |

## 2. Program structure and typed input

A TypeScript file is a JavaScript file with annotations. Run it with `ts-node`, `tsx`, Node's `--experimental-strip-types` (Node 22.6+, which supports *erasable* syntax only: no enums, no parameter properties), or compile with `tsc` and run the output. Enable `"strict": true` in `tsconfig.json`. Reading input is the same as in JavaScript; the annotation tells the compiler what you get back:

**How it works.** `readFileSync(0, "utf8")` returns a `string`; `.split(...)` gives `string[]`; `.filter(Boolean)` keeps the type; `.map(Number)` converts to `number[]`. The annotation `const data: number[]` is optional here (inferred) but documents the contract. Total cost is O(length of the input).

## 3. The type system in depth

### 3.1 Primitive and built-in types

| Type | Meaning | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `number` | any float (also integers) | exact integers only up to 2⁵³ - 1 |
| `bigint` | arbitrary-precision integer | `123n`; do not mix with `number` |
| `string`, `boolean` | as in JS | |
| `null`, `undefined` | the "no value" types | under `strict` they are **not** assignable to other types |
| `T[]`, `Array<T>` | arrays | `ReadonlyArray<T>` / `readonly T[]` forbids mutation |
| `[A, B]` | **tuple**: fixed length and types | `[number, string]`; named elements `[dist: number, node: number]` |
| `Map<K, V>`, `Set<T>` | typed collections | `map.get(k)` is `V | undefined` |
| `unknown` | "something, check before use" | the safe top type |
| `any` | opt out of checking | avoid |
| `never` | a value that cannot exist | for impossible branches and functions that always throw |
| `void` | no meaningful return value | |
| `object`, `{}` | any non-primitive / non-null value | rarely useful |

### 3.2 Inference and annotations
TypeScript **infers** types from initial values, so `let count = 5` is a `number` and `const mode = "fast"` has the **literal type** `"fast"`. Annotate **function parameters and return types** (the boundary of your code) and let local variables be inferred. Annotate when inference is too wide (`const a: number[] = []` instead of `never[]`).

### 3.3 Unions, intersections, literals and narrowing
* A **union** `A | B` is a value that is either type. Use it for "number or string", "result or error", "found or `undefined`".
* A **literal type** such as `"up"` restricts a value to specific constants; `type Dir = "up" | "down"` gives you an enum-like set without runtime cost.
* An **intersection** `A & B` has the members of both.
* **Narrowing:** inside `if (typeof x === "number")`, `if (x !== undefined)`, `if ("n" in x)`, `if (x instanceof Date)` or after checking a **tag** field, the compiler refines the union. A **discriminated union** (each variant has a literal `kind`) makes `switch` exhaustive, and a `never` check turns a forgotten case into a compile error.
* **Structural typing:** an object is acceptable wherever its *shape* matches, so `Person` works where `Named` is expected as long as it has a `name: string`.
* **`readonly`** properties and arrays cannot be modified through that type; `as const` freezes a literal to its narrowest readonly type. The utility types `Partial<T>`, `Required<T>`, `Readonly<T>`, `Pick<T, K>`, `Omit<T, K>`, `Record<K, V>` build new types from old ones.

Run the program, then uncomment each *compile error* line in your editor and read the message; that is the quickest way to learn the checker:
Inference, unions, narrowing, intersection, structural typing, readonly, discriminated unions and utility types

### 3.4 Strict null checks: the feature that pays for TypeScript
With `strictNullChecks`, `null` and `undefined` are separate types. A function that may not find something returns `T | undefined`, and you **must** handle it before using the value (`if (x !== undefined)`, `x ?? fallback`, `x?.field`). `Map.get`, `Array.find`, `array[i]` with `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`, and `string.match` all return possibly-missing values, which is exactly where JavaScript programs crash at run time. The non-null assertion `x!` tells the compiler "trust me"; use it only when you can prove the value exists (for example right after checking `has`).

### 3.5 Numbers, overflow and conversions
The runtime is JavaScript's: **all numbers are 64-bit floats**. There is no integer overflow, but integers above **2⁵³ - 1 lose precision**, so use `bigint` for exact huge values. Division is floating point (`7 / 2 === 3.5`); use `Math.floor` or `Math.trunc` for integer division. `%` keeps the dividend's sign. Bitwise operators work on **32-bit** signed integers. Convert strings explicitly: `Number(s)`, `Number.parseInt(s, 10)`; `Number("")` is `0`, `Number("12px")` is `NaN`. Truthiness and equality rules are those of JavaScript: use `===`, and remember `NaN !== NaN`.

## 4. Operators and control flow

The operators and statements are those of JavaScript: arithmetic `+ - * / % **`, comparison `=== !== < <= > >=`, logical `&& || !`, **nullish coalescing** `??`, **optional chaining** `?.`, bitwise `& | ^ ~ << >> >>>`, spread/rest `...`, destructuring. Control flow: `if`, `switch`, `for`, `for...of` (values), `for...in` (keys), `while`, `do...while`, `break`, `continue`, labels. TypeScript makes these safer: `for (const x of arr)` gives `x` the element type; a `switch` over a union can be checked for exhaustiveness; `??` only replaces `null`/`undefined` (so `0 ?? 5` is `0`).

**Counting the cost** is identical to JavaScript: a loop over n items is O(n); hidden linear work inside loops (`includes`, `indexOf`, `shift`, `slice`, spread) makes it O(n²).

## 5. Functions and generics in depth

Annotate parameters and the return type: `function sum(a: number[]): number`. Optional parameters (`x?: number`), default values (`k = 3`), rest parameters (`...xs: number[]`), function types `(a: number, b: number) => number`, overloads, and arrow functions all work. As in JavaScript, arguments are **passed by sharing**: the callee receives a copy of the value, which for arrays and objects is a reference to the same object, so it can mutate but not rebind the caller's variable; `readonly` parameter types document and enforce "I will not mutate this".

### 5.1 Generics
A **generic** function or class works over many types while staying type-safe: `function maxBy<T>(items: readonly T[], key: (t: T) => number): T | undefined`. The type parameter is *inferred* from the call. **Constraints** (`T extends HasLength`) say what a type argument must support. Generic classes such as `Stack<T>` and `MinHeap<T>` let you write a data structure once and have the compiler stop you from pushing a `string` into a `Stack<number>`.
Generics, constraints, a generic Stack and the safe unknown type

### 5.2 Recursion and stack depth
The runtime limit is the same as in JavaScript: roughly 10⁴ nested calls before `RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded`. Convert deep recursion to a loop with an explicit stack, and memoise with a `Map<string, number>` or an array.

## 6. Strings in depth

Strings are JavaScript strings: **immutable** UTF-16 sequences; `s[i]` is a one-character `string`. TypeScript types them as `string`, so a function taking a `string` rejects a `number` at compile time. The operations and costs are exactly those of JavaScript:

| Operation | Code | Time | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Length | `s.length` | O(1) | |
| Index | `s[i]`, `s.at(-1)` | O(1) | typed `string` (or `string | undefined` with `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`) |
| Char code | `s.charCodeAt(i)` | O(1) | letter index `s.charCodeAt(i) - 97` |
| Substring | `s.slice(a, b)` | O(b - a) | end exclusive |
| Concatenate | `s + t`, template literal | amortised cheap | build large strings with `join` |
| Compare | `s === t` | O(min(n, m)) | |
| Search | `indexOf`, `includes` | O(n·m) worst | |
| Split / join | `split`, `join` | O(n) | `split` returns `string[]` |
| Reverse | `[...s].reverse().join("")` | O(n) | |
| Space | | O(n) | |

**String literal types and template literal types** (`type Id = \`user-${number}\``) let the compiler check string *formats*, but that is rarely needed in algorithm problems.

## 7. Arrays in depth

A TypeScript array is a JavaScript array with an element type: `number[]`, `string[]`, `number[][]` for grids, `Array<[number, number]>` for pairs. The complexity table is the same as in JavaScript: index O(1), `push`/`pop` amortised O(1), `shift`/`unshift`/`splice` in the middle **O(n)**, `indexOf`/`includes` O(n), `sort` O(n log n) and **stable**, copying O(n). Use typed arrays (`Int32Array`, `Float64Array`) for fixed-size numeric data: contiguous and compact, 4 or 8 bytes per element. A `readonly number[]` parameter promises not to mutate. **`sort()` still sorts as strings by default**, so always write `(a, b) => a - b`. Grids: `Array.from({ length: r }, () => new Array<number>(c).fill(0))`; never `new Array(r).fill(new Array(c))`.

| Operation | Time | Space |
|---|---|---|
| `a[i]` read/write | O(1) | O(1) |
| `push` / `pop` | amortised O(1) / O(1) | O(1) |
| `shift` / `unshift` | **O(n)** | O(1) |
| `splice` in the middle | O(n) | O(k) |
| `indexOf` / `includes` / `find` | O(n) | O(1) |
| `slice` / spread copy | O(n) | O(n) |
| `sort` | O(n log n) | O(n) |
| `map` / `filter` | O(n) | O(n) |
Narrowing, defaults with ??, tuples and a discriminated union
Typed strings, counting array, grids and sorting

## 8. `Map` and `Set` in depth

`Map<K, V>` and `Set<T>` are the same hash tables as in JavaScript (insertion ordered, keys keep their type, objects compare by identity), now **typed**: `new Map<string, number>()` rejects `set("a", "x")`. `get(k)` has type `V | undefined`, which is the safe, honest type: handle the missing case.

| Operation | `Map` / `Set` | `Record<string, V>` / object |
|---|---|---|
| set / add | O(1) amortised | O(1) average |
| get / has | O(1) average | O(1) average |
| delete | O(1) average | O(1) average |
| size | O(1) | O(n) |
| iterate | O(n), insertion order | O(n) |
| space | O(n) | O(n) |

Keys that are arrays or objects are compared by **identity**; encode coordinates as a string `` `${r},${c}` `` or a number `r * cols + c`. A `Record<string, number>` is typed like an object but **all keys are strings**; prefer `Map<number, V>` for numeric keys. There is no built-in sorted map; keep a sorted array and binary search (O(log n) find, O(n) insert).
Typed Map and Set, coordinate keys and direction arrays

## 9. Stacks, queues, deques and heaps (typed)

| Structure | Implementation | Operations | Time | Space |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Stack | `T[]` with `push`/`pop`/`at(-1)` | push, pop, peek | O(1) each | O(n) |
| Queue | head-index class (`Queue<T>` below) | enqueue, dequeue | O(1) each (`shift` would be O(n)) | O(n) |
| Deque | two indexes over an array / linked list | both ends | O(1) each | O(n) |
| Heap | generic `MinHeap<T>` with a comparator | push, pop, peek | O(log n), O(log n), O(1) | O(n) |
| Sorted set | sorted `T[]` + binary search | find, insert | O(log n), O(n) | O(n) |

**How the heap works.** A complete binary tree stored in an array: element `i` has children `2i + 1`, `2i + 2` and parent `(i - 1) >> 1`. **Push** appends and *sifts up* (at most log n swaps). **Pop** removes the root, moves the last element to the root, and *sifts down* (at most log n swaps). **Peek** is the root. **Heapify** n items takes O(n). A **max**-heap just flips the comparator. The generic class below is typed so that `MinHeap<[number, number]>` accepts only `(distance, node)` pairs; note it avoids *parameter properties* so Node's type stripping can run it.
Generic MinHeap, stack and a head-index Queue

## 10. Sorting, comparators and searching

A comparator has type `(a: T, b: T) => number`. Describe record shapes with an `interface` so that a misspelt field is a compile error, and chain keys with `||`: `(a, b) => b.age - a.age || a.name.localeCompare(b.name)`. `sort` is **stable**, sorts **in place**, and without a comparator converts elements to strings. Binary search is a hand-written `lo/hi` loop (no built-in); typing the array as `readonly number[]` documents that it is not modified.
Typed comparators and a typed lowerBound

## 11. Objects, classes and the memory model

Classes add **type information** to JavaScript classes: field types, `private`/`protected`/`public`/`readonly` modifiers (enforced only at compile time, except `#private`), `implements` for interfaces, and generics. Objects are heap references; equality and hashing are by identity. The garbage collector frees unreachable objects.

### 11.1 Linked lists and trees
Model nodes with an `interface` (or class) whose links are **nullable**: `next: ListNode | null`. Strict null checks then force you to test `node !== null` before dereferencing, removing the classic "cannot read property of null" crash. Reaching the i-th node is O(i); inserting after a node you hold is O(1); recursion depth equals tree height.
Interfaces for nodes and an adjacency-list type

### 11.2 Graphs
An **adjacency list** `number[][]` (or `Edge[][]` with `{ to, w }` for weighted edges) uses O(V + E) space; an adjacency matrix `number[][]` uses O(V²). Breadth-first search with a head-index queue visits each vertex and edge once: **O(V + E) time, O(V) space**, shortest paths in an unweighted graph.
A typed adjacency list and breadth-first search

## 12. Errors and edge cases

TypeScript catches *some* edge cases at compile time (a possibly-`undefined` value, a missing union case) and none at run time (empty arrays, `NaN`, division by zero, deep recursion). With `strict` on, `catch (e)` gives `e` the type `unknown`: narrow it (`e instanceof Error`) before using `.message`. Model expected failures as **values** with a `Result<T>` union, and reserve `throw` for genuine programming errors.

| Edge case | Typical bug | Defence |
|---|---|---|
| Empty array | `a[0]` is `undefined`; `Math.max(...[])` is `-Infinity` | check `a.length === 0` |
| Missing `Map` key | `get` is `V | undefined` | `?? 0`, or check `has` |
| `Number("")` is 0 | silent wrong value | trim and test for `""` |
| Huge integers | precision loss above 2⁵³ - 1 | `bigint`, `Number.isSafeInteger` |
| Forgotten union case | silent fall-through | `never` exhaustiveness check |
| `sort()` with no comparator | string order | `(a, b) => a - b` |
A Result type, never, unknown in catch, empty input and exhaustive checks

## 13. The master complexity cheat sheet

`n` is the number of elements. Running time is that of JavaScript; types add none.

| Operation | `T[]` | typed array | `Map<K,V>` / `Set<T>` | `Record` / object | `string` | `MinHeap<T>` |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Access by index / key | O(1) | O(1) | O(1) avg | O(1) avg | O(1) | peek O(1) |
| Push / pop at end | O(1)* / O(1) | n/a | n/a | n/a | n/a | O(log n) |
| Shift / unshift (front) | **O(n)** | n/a | n/a | n/a | n/a | n/a |
| Insert / delete in the middle | O(n) | n/a | O(1) avg by key | O(1) avg | O(n) | n/a |
| Search by value | O(n) | O(n) | O(1) avg by key | O(1) avg by key | O(n·m) | O(n) |
| Min / max | O(n) | O(n) | O(n) | O(n) | O(n) | O(1) |
| Sort | O(n log n) | O(n log n) | n/a | n/a | via array | n/a |
| Iterate | O(n) | O(n) | O(n) | O(n) | O(n) | O(n) |
| Space | O(n) | 4 or 8 B per item | O(n), heavier | O(n), heavier | O(n) | O(n) |

\* amortised or average.

**What to say in an interview:** "I'll keep a `Map<number, number>` from value to index. Each lookup and insert is O(1) on average, so one pass is O(n) time and O(n) extra space. The brute force is O(n²) time and O(1) space; I'm trading memory for time. And because `get` returns `number | undefined`, the compiler makes me handle the missing case."

## 14. Pitfalls and idioms checklist

1. Turn on `strict`; avoid `any` and the `!` assertion unless you can justify them.
2. `map.get(k)` is `V | undefined`: handle it with `??`, `if` or `?.`.
3. `sort()` without a comparator still sorts as strings.
4. Types are **erased**: you cannot test an interface at run time; use a tag field or `typeof`/`in`/`instanceof`.
5. `number` is a float: integers lose exactness above 2⁵³ - 1; use `bigint`.
6. `shift()` is O(n): use a head index.
7. Prefer `unknown` to `any` for untrusted data, then validate.
8. Use `readonly` for inputs you will not mutate.
9. Use discriminated unions plus a `never` check for exhaustive handling.
10. `catch (e)` is `unknown`: narrow before use.
11. Object keys are strings; use `Map` for numbers.
12. Do not use `enum` if you want Node's type stripping; use union literals or `as const` objects.
13. Equal arrays are not equal keys: encode them.
14. Recursion depth is about 10⁴: convert to loops.

## 15. A reusable solution template
Template: typed pure function plus input and output

## 16. How TypeScript compares with the other languages in this chapter

| Topic | TypeScript | JavaScript | Java | C# |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Typing | static, structural, erased | dynamic | static, nominal | static, nominal |
| Null safety | `strictNullChecks` | none | `Optional`, annotations | nullable reference types |
| Integers | float / `bigint` | same | 32/64-bit | 32/64-bit |
| Generics | yes (erased) | n/a | yes (erased) | yes (reified) |
| Heap | write your own | write your own | `PriorityQueue` | `PriorityQueue` |
| Runtime | JavaScript engine | same | JVM | .NET |

## 17. Practice plan

1. Convert your JavaScript solutions to TypeScript and fix every compiler error: each one is a bug you would otherwise ship.
2. Re-type the generic `MinHeap<T>` and `Queue<T>` until you can write them from memory.
3. Solve [Pair With Target Sum](/problems/pair-with-target-sum), [Kth Largest](/problems/kth-largest), [Shortest Maze Path](/problems/shortest-maze-path) and [Course Order](/problems/course-order) in TypeScript, writing the type of every function first, then the time and space complexity.

lessons.title: Big-O in plain words
lessons.md:
## Why we measure growth

Two programs can both be correct and still behave very differently when the input grows. **Big-O notation** describes how the work an algorithm does *grows* with the input size `n`, ignoring constant factors.

| Growth | Name | Doubling `n` makes the work... |
|---|---|---|
| O(1) | constant | the same |
| O(log n) | logarithmic | one step longer |
| O(n) | linear | twice as long |
| O(n log n) | linearithmic | slightly more than twice |
| O(n²) | quadratic | four times as long |

We usually talk about the **worst case** and drop everything but the fastest-growing term: `3n² + 10n + 7` is just O(n²).
lessons.tip: Memory counts too. The fast version trades O(n) extra space for speed.

quiz.explanation: (2n)² = 4n².

quiz.explanation: Only the growth rate matters.

## Cases and memory

The **best case** is the luckiest input, the **worst case** the unluckiest, and the **average case** a typical one. Linear search finds its target immediately in the best case (O(1)) and scans everything in the worst case (O(n)). Interviews usually mean the worst case unless stated.

**Space complexity** counts the extra memory you use besides the input. A hash set of `n` items is O(n) space; swapping in place is O(1). Recursion uses stack space proportional to its depth.

quiz.explanation: It is measured with the same Big-O notation.

## Putting things in order

| Algorithm | Idea | Time (typical) |
|---|---|---|
| Bubble / selection / insertion | simple comparisons and swaps | O(n²) |
| Merge sort | split, sort halves, merge | O(n log n) |
| Quick sort | partition around a pivot | O(n log n) average |
| Counting sort | count occurrences of small integers | O(n + k) |

**Insertion sort** is fast on nearly sorted data. **Merge sort** is stable and predictable. In practice use your language's built-in sort (O(n log n)) and focus on *what to sort by*.

lessons.md:
## The O(n²) trio

- **Bubble sort** swaps adjacent out-of-order pairs; the largest item floats to the end each pass.
- **Selection sort** repeatedly selects the minimum of the unsorted part and swaps it into place.
- **Insertion sort** grows a sorted prefix by inserting each new item where it belongs; excellent on nearly sorted input.

They are simple and in place; use them to understand sorting, not for large inputs.

quiz.explanation: It does one comparison per element.

## Partition around a pivot

**Quick sort** picks a pivot, moves smaller items left and larger right, then sorts both sides: O(n log n) on average, O(n²) in the worst case (mitigate by random pivots). **Quickselect** uses the same partition to find the k-th smallest element in average O(n) without fully sorting.

## The workhorse structure

An **array** stores items in consecutive memory, so reading `a[i]` is O(1). Appending at the end is amortised O(1); inserting or deleting in the middle is O(n) because later items shift.

A frequent technique is the **write index**: scan with one index and keep another where the next kept value goes. It filters or compacts an array in place with O(1) extra space.

quiz.explanation: Every existing item has to shift one place.

- **Majority element:** the voting idea keeps a candidate and a counter in O(1) space.
- **Missing number in 0..n:** the sum formula `n(n+1)/2` minus the actual sum.
- **Reverse in place:** swap from both ends moving inward.

Most of these are a single scan; think about what **state** you need to carry from one element to the next.

## Strings are sequences

A string is a sequence of characters. In most languages strings are **immutable**: building one by repeated `+=` in a loop copies each time and can be O(n²); collect pieces in a list and join once.

Useful moves: iterate by index, compare characters from both ends (palindromes), count characters with an array of 26 or a map, and slice carefully (check off-by-one at the boundaries).

## Constant-time lookups

A **hash map** stores key to value pairs. A hash function turns a key into a bucket number, so insert, lookup and delete are **average O(1)**. Collisions (two keys in one bucket) are handled by chaining or probing.

### The classic trade
Whenever a nested loop asks *"have I seen a matching value?"*, a hash map usually turns it into a single pass at the cost of O(n) memory.
